Regarding the fact that mental karma is exclusively non-informative (*avijñapti*): mental karma possesses only the nature of the non-informative; it is not like the informative (*vijñapti*) form. Because this karma cannot be demonstrated to others, it is called "non-informative."
Because it possesses verbal expression, it is called "informative" (vijñapti).
Among these five types of action, one should know that informative action is of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Mental karma is also like this; others are not said to be neutral (*avyākṛta*).

It should be known that informative [karma] (*vijñapti*) is of three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral; that is, bodily informative action and vocal informative action should be known as being of these three kinds.
"Wholesome" refers to bodily action initiated by a wholesome mind, such as the practice of giving or receiving the precepts.
"Unwholesome" refers to bodily action initiated by an unwholesome mind, such as killing.
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is of two kinds: obscured (*nivṛta*) and unobscured (*anivṛta*).
The obscured refers to bodily movement initiated by a defiled indeterminate mind.
The unobscured refers to bodily movement initiated by a non-defiled indeterminate mind, namely, deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
One should know that verbal instruction is also like this.
Regarding "mental action is also like this," mental action likewise has three types:

that which is associated with a wholesome mind is necessarily wholesome; that which is associated with an unwholesome mind is called unwholesome; and that which is associated with a defiled indeterminate mind is necessarily obscured-indeterminate, while that which is associated with a non-defiled indeterminate mind is called non-obscured-indeterminate.
Regarding the statement that "the others are not said to be indeterminate": there are two other types of karma, namely the non-informative (avijñapti) karma of body and speech.
These are of two kinds—wholesome and unwholesome—but they are never indeterminate.
Why is this? Because it is weak.
Since the indeterminate mind is weak, it cannot give rise to powerful karma.
If it coexists with other consciousnesses and continues as that object, it is like grasping a *sumana* flower: even after one lets go of it, its fragrance still lingers. Why is this?
Because the continuity of fragrance arises, it is not like [the case of] grasping at wood, stone, and so forth.
The various types of karma have already been explained.
There are two kinds of neutral matter (*rūpa-avyākṛta*): the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*).
The obscured [unwholesome] is bound to the form realm; the remainder exists in two realms.

Regarding the two types of neutral form—the obscured and the non-obscured: as for the nature of form, karma, and instruction, the term "neutral" has already been explained previously. One should know that this [neutral form] is of two kinds: the obscured and the non-obscured.
Regarding "those obscured [factors] bound to the form realm": if they are obscured, they are bound to the Brahma-world of the form realm, not to the higher stages.
Why is this? Because those [higher stages] lack the mind of volitional activity; thus, the afflictions of a lower stage do not arise and manifest within a higher stage.
Why is this? Because they are free from desire.
Furthermore, one does not abide in the realm of desire while cultivating the path to sever the afflictions that give rise to bodily and vocal karma.
Why is this? Because they operate through the external gates.
Since the afflictions abandoned by the Path of Seeing function through the internal gates, they cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma.

The afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*); afflictions that are not unwholesome cannot give rise to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma.
As for those remaining in the two realms [the form and formless realms], if they are non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), they are bound to both the desire and form realms.
Mental karma is explained in the same way as the mind.
Why? Because those [types of karma], whether obscured or unobscured, pertain to all three realms.
Within this context:
If one speaks briefly of the precepts of both informative and non-informative action, there are three types:
those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), those born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja*), and those based on the precepts conducive to liberation (*prātimokṣa-samvara*).

Regarding the statement that "if one briefly explains the unmanifest precepts (avijñapti-śīla), there are three kinds," it should be understood that the unmanifest precepts, when briefly explained, indeed consist of three kinds.
Question: What are they?
Answer: The untainted (*anāsrava*) and those born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja*) depend upon the precepts conducive to liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*).
The untainted precepts arise simultaneously with the Path; they consist of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Precepts born of dhyāna arise simultaneously with dhyāna; these belong to both ordinary persons—whether they have abandoned desire or not—and to noble ones.
Precepts based on and conforming to the discipline of liberation (prātimokṣa-saṃvara) are those obtained by requesting them from another person within a gathered assembly.
These three types of precepts encompass all precepts.
Question: Thus has the analysis of the precepts consisting of informative and non-informative action been completed.
What arises simultaneously with the mind?
What does not arise simultaneously with the mind?
The answer is:
Non-informative action (avijñapti) exists in the desire realm; informative action (vijñapti) depends on the two realms of existence.
One should know that it does not coexist with the mind; as for the others, they are said to coexist with the mind.

Whether the non-informative action of the desire realm is included within the vows conducive to liberation or is not so included, all of it does not coexist with the mind, in the sense that it does not follow the fluctuations of the mind.
Question: For what reason does it not follow the mind? Answer:

Because after he has received the precepts, unwholesome and neutral minds also arise accordingly, [the precepts] do not function in conjunction with wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral minds. Why is this?
Because they also proceed even in the absence of mind.
As for the teaching, [the factors] of the desire and form realms do not proceed in accordance with the mind. Why is this?
Because it belongs to the body, other minds also possess it.

That is to say, regarding the statement that they are concomitant with other minds: "other" refers to dhyāna-restraint and untainted (anāsrava) restraint; these two types follow the movement of the mind.
Why is this? Because they do not follow and transform along with a different mind.
Since the power of that [original] mind gives rise to these two types, they constantly act in accordance with the mind, following its meaning.
Regarding those two types, the past is accomplished as past, the future is accomplished as future, and the present is accomplished as present.
Having explained the distinctions among karmas, I shall now explain the accomplishment of karma.
The untainted (anāsrava) restraint of the precepts is accomplished through seeing reality;
that born of dhyāna is attained when one obtains dhyāna; and that born of maintaining the precepts arises in the desire realm.

Regarding "the untainted restraint of the precepts is accomplished through seeing reality": this refers to the accomplishment of untainted precepts from the initial stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) by all noble ones (ārya). These precepts reside in six stages:
The preparatory, intermediate, and fundamental stages of the four dhyānas—these levels of form are also untainted (*anāsrava*).
One who has not yet abandoned desire, having accomplished the vision of the truths, possesses the morality of the preparatory stage.
If one is free from desire, all those in training (śaikṣa) achieve at least three stages, or perhaps six; all arhats achieve six stages.
Regarding "if one attains dhyāna through birth in dhyāna," this refers to the accomplishment of the dhyāna-precepts and nothing else.
These precepts exist in nine stages, namely: the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of dhyāna, the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the four dhyānas.
Whether it be a person who has attained the various stages (bhūmi), or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), or a noble one (ārya)—all such individuals achieve the precepts of those respective stages.
For those who uphold the precepts and are born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), if they have received the vows, they achieve the *anuloma-vimukti-śīla* (precepts conducive to liberation).
This precept is obtained by persons of the desire realm and is not received by those in other destinies.

Having briefly explained the distinctions in its accomplishment, we shall now discuss the three types of persons according to their accomplishment of past, future, and present precepts: namely, the person abiding in morality, the person abiding in immorality, and the person abiding in neither morality nor immorality.
Those who abide in morality are also of three kinds, because there are three kinds of morality.
As for them: if one abides in the morality of liberation (*prātimokṣa-śīla*), that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is present.
It should be known that one always accomplishes it, or else accomplishes it as entirely past.

Regarding the statement, "If one abides in the *prātimokṣa* discipline, it should be known that one always accomplishes its non-informative (*avijñapti*) aspect in the present": if one abides in the *prātimokṣa* discipline conducive to liberation, from the very first moment of receiving the non-informative precepts, that person accomplishes those present non-informative factors at all times; they constantly continue in succession until life has not yet ended.
Why is this? Because it is defined by its specific temporal limits.

Alternatively, for one who has completed [the vow] in the past, there may be those who abide in the *anuloma-vimukti-śīla* (precepts conducive to liberation) and have accomplished the past *avijñapti-śīla* (unmanifest precept), meaning that which has already ceased but has not been relinquished.
There are five causes and conditions for the relinquishing of an action, which will be explained later.
If one performs an act of instruction and achieves it during the intermediate period,
and that [action] is exhausted without being relinquished, one should know that it becomes past.
If one performs an act of instruction and achieves it during the middle period— where "middle period" refers to the present—
then when a person performs an act of body or speech as an instruction while seeking to receive the precepts, they achieve the present instruction-precept (*vijñapti-śīla*).
"One should know that when it has been exhausted but not relinquished, it constitutes the past. Here, "exhausted" means "past.
If one does not relinquish those teachings at the time they are exhausted, one fulfills the past teaching-precepts.
The causes and conditions for this relinquishment are as previously explained.
To state it briefly: at the time of the initial moment of instruction, one accomplishes both present instruction (*vijñapti*) and non-instruction (*avijñapti*).
Thereafter, until that instruction has ceased in the future, one accomplishes both past and present instruction and non-instruction.
If one does not abandon this teaching after it has been exhausted, one accomplishes past and present non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Such a person, however, accomplishes only past informative action (*vijñapti*), not present informative action.
If one attains dhyāna without informative intimation (*avijñapti*), one achieves the cessation of the future;
if one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the interim, informative intimation is also as previously explained.
Regarding "if one attains dhyāna without informative intimation, one achieves the cessation of the future": if one attains dhyāna, one achieves the past and future dhyāna-precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*).
Just as when one has attained dhyāna, although the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) of that person is certainly extinguished, by the power of that dhyāna, they initially attain it in the past.

As with dhyāna, from the second moment onward, one attains it across the three times until the dhyāna has not yet arisen; if it arises and is not relinquished, one attains the past and future untainted (anāsrava) morality.
Because it is identical to dhyāna, it is not discussed here;
since the precepts of dhyāna have already been explained, those [precepts] have also been explained. Why is this so?

If there is one who has seen the teaching of the Truths, that person will certainly attain the precepts of dhyāna; therefore, when the precepts of dhyāna are spoken of, it is he who is being described.

If one performs unwholesome karma, yet abides in the precepts and accomplishes both [the mundane and supramundane], though they coexist with the entanglements of the afflictions, one should know that those [afflictions] are utterly exhausted.

If one performs unwholesome karma while abiding in the accomplishment of both [types of] morality: if a person abides in the morality conducive to liberation or abides in the dhyāna-morality, yet has not seen the Truths, then when an intense obsession with the unwholesome arises, unwholesome non-informative action (avijñapti) immediately originates; at that time, that person accomplishes both unwholesome informative action (vijñapti) and non-informative action.
Question: What is it that, while abiding in the precepts of dhyāna, performs unwholesome deeds? Answer:
If one has not yet abandoned desire, one may perform unwholesome actions based on the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamyadhyāna).
Question: At what time is the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) accomplished?
Answer: It is associated with the entanglements of affliction.
One should know that for such a person, as long as they have not yet abandoned the unwholesome entanglements, those [afflictions] will continue to exhaust until they are completely exhausted.
If one abandons those envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), both the informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) [karma] are also abandoned.
If one abides in a state that is neither moral nor immoral, while possessing non-informative karma,
one should know that its fruit is undesirable, or else it has already perished in the past.

Regarding the statement that one who dwells in a state of non-restraint should be known as possessing unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*) which yields undesirable fruits: "one who dwells in non-restraint" refers to those such as sheep-butchers, poultry-slayers, pork-butchers, fishermen, bird-catchers, and so forth. Such persons, at all times, possess present unwholesome non-informative action.

At the very moment this person first initiates the action, they simultaneously acquire the non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) comprised within unwholesome discipline (aśīla) toward all sentient beings.
When a person first commits killing, they immediately acquire the non-informative [matter] comprised within that act of killing.
Thereafter, in accordance with each subsequent act of killing, one further acquires the non-informative matter (avijñapti) subsumed under killing.
However, because the precepts subsumed under the restraint (saṃvara) have already been acquired previously, they are not acquired again.

Alternatively, regarding "exhausting the past": from the second moment onward, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) comprised by killing and non-restraint is both accomplished and present; it is called "exhausted" when it has passed away into the past without being relinquished at any given moment.
If the teaching on momentary abiding is said to be within the context of accomplishment, it likewise exhausts the past; this is contrary to the superior [view].

If the teaching on momentary abiding is said to be within the context of accomplishment, then according to the time of the teaching on abiding, one accomplishes the present teaching; that which is present for a single moment is called "momentary abiding."

Regarding "having also exhausted those of the past": as long as they have not been abandoned since their exhaustion in the past according to the teaching—that is, while they have not yet been severed—one accomplishes both the past and the present; however, if they are exhausted but not yet abandoned, one accomplishes only the past.

Regarding that which is the opposite of the aforementioned: as it was stated that one abiding in restraint performs unwholesome [actions], so too is it said that one abiding in non-restraint performs wholesome [actions].

When one performs wholesome acts such as giving with extremely pure faith, at that time wholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises; when that [faith] is abandoned, this [non-informative matter] is also abandoned.
If performed in a neutral state, this is said to be accomplished in the neutral;
it also exhausts the past, whether two or even one.
Regarding "if performed in a neutral state, this is said to be accomplished in the neutral": "neutral" refers to that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
If he performs wholesome deeds, he accomplishes the present wholesome teaching;
if he performs unwholesome deeds, he accomplishes the present unwholesome teaching.
Furthermore, regarding those that are exhausted in the past: if this teaching has ceased but is not yet severed, one also accomplishes both the past and the present.
If, after it has been exhausted, one does not relinquish it, one merely accomplishes the past;

or both [the past and present], whether it be informative (vijñapti) or non-informative (avijñapti), provided that one intends to act with extreme zeal and certainly does not relinquish the preparatory effort (prayoga).
Furthermore, there is another case: once the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has ceased, one achieves only the present non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
There are those who, until their lives come to an end, achieve the present non-informative action because they have no desire to stop it.
Question: You have already explained the precepts for training that accord with liberation.
How are the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts obtained?
The answer is:
Within the realm of form, the wholesome mind attains the precepts of dhyāna-restraint;
when that [dhyāna] is relinquished, those [precepts] are also relinquished. The untainted [mind] consists of six types of consciousness.

Regarding those who obtain the restraint of dhyāna (dhyāna-saṃvara) through a wholesome mind in the form realm: if a person attains a wholesome mind of the form realm—whether at times they are free from desire or not—they all obtain the restraint of dhyāna.

In all realms of form (*rūpadhātu*), the wholesome mind is constantly accompanied by ethical discipline (*śīla*), with the sole exception of six types of consciousness: namely, the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as [the mental consciousness associated with] hearing and wisdom (*śrutamayī prajñā*).
When the mind approaches the end of life, the mind gives rise to karmic activity. A question is asked:
"How is this relinquished?
The answer is:
When that is relinquished, this is also relinquished.
If one relinquishes the wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one also relinquishes that [uncontaminated mind].

Regarding the six uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*): those who possess the uncontaminated precepts acquire them together with these six minds—namely, the *anāgāmya*, the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas. When those are relinquished, these are also relinquished.
Question: Regarding these various precepts, which ones are they?
At what time are they relinquished?
The answer is:
The discipline of conformity to liberation abandons [the precepts] during five periods;
the meditative absorption-born and the outflow-free precepts are taught by wisdom during two periods.

Regarding "the discipline of liberation through conformity is relinquished at five times," this refers to relinquishment at the time of abandoning one's own class [of beings], at the time of abandoning the precepts, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, at the time of the arising of both sexual organs, and at the time of the disappearance of the True Dharma.
Some say that one abandons the precepts at the root of a transgression or when practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Those from Kaśmīra say there are four occasions for abandonment, excluding the latter two types.

Regarding the untainted precepts born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which are spoken of by the wise as being abandoned on two occasions: these are the two occasions for abandoning the precepts of meditative concentration.
The untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are also relinquished at two times:
through falling away and through attaining a fruit.
Since those faculties obtain fruits in a sequence that is similar [to their acquisition], they are not explained separately.
Some distinguish them by stating that those three are abandoned at three different times. Question:
How is non-restraint abandoned?
The answer is:
Non-restraint is abandoned at four times; likewise for wholesome formless states.
Defilement occurs at only one time; this is said to reside in the mind.

Regarding the four times when non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) does not exist: namely, at the time of receiving the precepts, at the time of attaining the dhyāna-precepts, at the time of the arising of both sexual organs, and at the time of abandoning one's own category.
That morality and non-morality are abandoned at three times: namely, when the original force has passed, when the aspiration has ceased, and when the application of effort has ended.
This is called the abandonment of morality and non-morality; it should be examined accordingly.
Question: The intrinsic nature and function of form have already been explained.
What, then, are the intrinsic nature and function of the formless?
Answer: It is thus with wholesome formless [states].

Wholesome formless karma is also relinquished at four times: namely, at the time of attaining the fruit, at the time of falling away, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, and at the time of transcending the realm or stage.

Regarding the statement that "defilement exists only at one time and resides in the mind": defiled mental karma is abandoned at one time, namely at the moment of detachment from desire; wherever one becomes detached from desire, there that [karma] is abandoned.
The intrinsic nature and the accomplishment of karma have already been explained.
Now, the Blessed One’s various classifications of that karma shall be discussed.
If a karma results in the fruit of suffering, one should know it to be unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*).
Furthermore, there are unwholesome mental actions: greed, hatred, and wrong view.

One should know that those karmas which result in bitter fruits are unwholesome actions; those karmas which bring about undesirable results are unwholesome actions. This refers to all unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma—such as killing and so forth—along with their subsequent attendants; these are called unwholesome actions.
Because obscured-unspecified states lack karmic fruition, they are not described as unwholesome conduct.
Furthermore, regarding those mental unwholesome conducts consisting of greed, hatred, and wrong view, these are unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*), as previously explained.

Furthermore, there are categories of karma consisting of greed, hatred, and wrong views; one should know that these are like [the aforementioned] karma, because the cause is established by means of the fruit, just as a woman is a defilement for the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
These and other such points have already been explained.
The opposite of those [unwholesome] actions is what the Most Victorious One has taught;
among these, when they are predominant, the Noble One speaks of the ten paths of action.

Regarding "the opposite of those actions is what the Most Victorious One has taught": this means that being the opposite of unwholesome conduct, they should all be known as wholesome conduct—namely, all wholesome karma, including mental karma consisting of non-greed, non-hatred, and right view.

Among these, when the Noble Ones speak of the ten courses of action as being predominant, they are called "courses of action" (karmapatha) because, within the context of wholesome and unwholesome actions, those that are particularly powerful and superior are designated by this name.
Among those unwholesome actions, those that are predominant are called unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*);
if they are predominant among wholesome actions, they are wholesome courses of action.
Unwholesome courses of action refer to the seven types beginning with killing, as well as covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
The paths of wholesome action refer to the seven types beginning with abstaining from killing, as well as non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
This is stated because either the preparatory application is predominant rather than the path of action itself, or the path of action itself is predominant. Thus it is said.
Taking life means: regarding another living being as such, forming the intention to kill, and employing the means to take their life; when that action is completed, it is called taking life.

Taking what is not given means: regarding another's property as another's property, with the thought that it has not been given and the intention to seize it by force, one takes possession of it for oneself; this is called taking what is not given.

Mistaken conduct (*mithyācāra*) refers to engaging in sexual activity in an improper place, with an improper person, or at an improper time; such engagement in what is not the proper sphere of conduct is called mistaken conduct.
False speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) refers to uttering words with a deceptive intent, speaking to another while harboring a different thought; this is called false speech.
Divisive speech is the verbal karma of one with a defiled mind who desires to cause dissension; this is called divisive speech.
Harsh speech is the utterance of words that others do not love, motivated by a mind of anger and resentment; this is called harsh speech.
Being brought to a standstill by weak views, craving, and so forth; unwholesome speech, useless speech, and speech contrary to the Dharma—this is called idle chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
As for greed (*lobha*): it is the longing for another’s property and covetousness; this is what is meant by greed.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) refers to the mental fault of excessive malice toward others and the destruction of them; this is called hatred.
Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) refers to the denial of cause and effect; this is called wrong view.
These are the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).
Those that are contrary to these are called wholesome paths of action (*kuśalakarmapatha*).

Other actions are not designated as "paths of action," namely: the preliminary efforts (*prayoga*) preceding these paths of action; unwholesome conduct such as drinking alcohol, beating, and striking; and wholesome conduct such as prostrating. Furthermore, the volition (*cetanā*) involved in abstaining from drinking alcohol—such instances are considered "action" (*karman*) but not "paths of action."
Question: What is the meaning of "paths of action" (karmapatha)? Answer:

These are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) because they are both actions and paths; furthermore, they are called "paths of action" because they are the paths of action; and they are called "paths of action" because they are the paths for the paths of action.
The seven [unwholesome] actions are both actions and paths, because they are the paths of volition (*cetanā*);
the three [unwholesome] paths of action are paths of action, but this does not mean they are themselves actions.
Question: For what reason, among all the afflictions (*kleśa*), are these three—greed and the others—designated as paths of action (*karmapatha*) and not the others? Answer:
Because it is an intensified evil and because one's own afflictions cause harm to others, this is an extreme transgression; other [paths] are not like this.
Its antidote—the white path of non-attachment and so forth—is included within these courses of action (*karmapatha*), whereas other [antidotes] are not.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds: namely, determinate and indeterminate.
The determinate has two types:
determinate in terms of retribution and determinate in terms of time.
There are three kinds of meditative concentration at that time. Question: What are they?
The answer is:
That which is called karma with fruit in the present life, next receives the fruit of rebirth, and the subsequent fruit is likewise; one should know that the timing for each is fixed.
If karma is performed in this life and ripens in that very same life, it is called karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*).
If karma ripens in the immediately following life, it is called karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*).
Karma that ripens in subsequent lives after the next is called "karma to be experienced later.
These three types are termed "determined by time.

Regarding "determined by retribution," this refers to karma whose retribution is certain to ripen, though it is not determined by time; if the necessary causes and conditions are encountered, it will then ripen.
The remainder are called indeterminate. Question:
As the Blessed One has taught, there are three types of karma, such as pleasant feeling and so forth.
What is the distinction?
The answer is:
wholesome karma within the desire realm, as well as that of the three stages of the form realm.
This is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); this too is both determinate (*niyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*).

Regarding the wholesome karma of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the three stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are called pleasant feeling: wholesome karma in the desire realm can produce a retribution (*vipāka*) accompanied by pleasure, and in the stages of the first, second, and third dhyānas of the form realm, it likewise produces a retribution accompanied by pleasure; these are collectively termed pleasant feeling.
Question: Is this karma also fixed in terms of time? Answer:
This is also either determinate or indeterminate;

whether determinate or indeterminate, the wholesome karma within these four stages is all termed "pleasant feeling. Because this is the retribution subsumed under pleasant feeling, it is called "pleasant feeling."
"Born into neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, that which exists in the higher good;
if one receives a painful retribution, this is called unwholesome karma.

Regarding "born into neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, that which exists in the higher good": wholesome karma of the fourth dhyāna and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is termed "neither-suffering-nor-pleasure feeling" (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*), because such karma is capable of producing a retribution associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
If it is said that experiencing a bitter retribution refers to unwholesome karma, this means that unwholesome karma is termed "bitter feeling.
Since that karma can produce a retribution associated with bitter feeling, such karma is likewise both determinate and indeterminate.
Question: As the Blessed One has taught regarding the four types of karma, such as black karma with black retribution and so forth,
how are they to be distinguished?
The answer is:
If it is wholesome karma within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is white and has a white retribution;
that which is black-and-white exists within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); and the two types of black are said to be impure.
If wholesome karma in the form realm is white and has a white retribution, it is because wholesome karma in the form realm is white, as it is entirely free from affliction;
its retribution is also white, as it is entirely desirable.

Regarding "black-and-white within the realm of desire": because wholesome karma in the realm of desire is interspersed with unwholesome karma, it is called "black-and-white. However, there is no single karma therein that results in a mixed reception of both black and white retributions.
Question: If the retribution is not black, why is it called black? Answer:
Because it is not loved, it is called "black"; that which is loved is called "white.
Regarding the two types of black described as impure: unwholesome karma is called black because it is not desirable, and that black karma produces black retribution in return.
If volition can destroy those various accomplished karmas and is associated with the path of non-obstruction, this is called the fourth karma.

If the path can sever those three types of karma—namely, the seventeen types of training volitions subsumed under the path of non-obstruction—this is the fourth karma; because it cannot be censured, it is called "not black."
Because it is free from defiled attachment, it is called "not white";
because it is contrary to the process of saṃsāra, it is called "without retribution.
It is subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge within the path of seeing.

The four volitions associated with the [four] paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and the eight volitions associated with the eight paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the desire realm—these twelve volitions sever karma that yields exclusively black retribution.
The single volition associated with the ninth path of non-obstruction severs karma that yields both black and white retribution.
The abandonment of desire from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna is subsumed under the ninth path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
The four associated volitions (*cetanā*) constitute white-with-white-retribution karma (*śukla-śuklavipāka-karma*). All other [karmas] are not retribution-producing karma (*avipāka-karma*).
Wholesome karma of the formless realm is not counted here.
Why is this? Because there are no two types of "white" (śukla) phenomena—namely, the white of purity and the white of being delightful—and therefore it is not described as white.
In this sutra, the Blessed One speaks of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
A question is asked:
As the Blessed One has taught regarding the crookedness, faults, and harshness of bodily, vocal, and mental karma; [how does this relate to the intermediate state?]
What are these? The answer is:
Deceit arises and is called crookedness; transgression arises from hatred.
The Blessed One has taught that desire gives rise to coarseness;
he taught that deceit gives rise to crookedness. To deceive others through artifice and to conceal one's own affairs—this mental crookedness is called deceit.
This exists in the desire realm and the Brahma-world, but not in the higher stages.
It resides in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*) and is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If karma arises from guile (*śāṭhya*), it is called "crooked" (*vaṅka*) by the Blessed One because the cause is established by means of the fruit; however, that [karma] does not possess the nature of crookedness itself.
Regarding "that which arises from hatred": karma arises from hatred; because the cause is expressed through its effect, the Blessed One spoke of it as "arising from hatred.
Regarding "that which arises from desire is called harsh": if karma arises from desire, the cause is spoken of within the effect; therefore, the Blessed One spoke of it as "harsh."
Question: As the World-Honored One has taught, there are three kinds of purity and three kinds of tranquility.
What are their characteristics?
The answer is:
All sublime conduct is pure; the body and speech of one beyond training are pure.
That which is called purity of mind is precisely the mind of one beyond training.
"Regarding 'all pure sublime conduct' (sarva-sucarita-śuddha): all sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), is said to be pure.
Question: Sublime conduct that is with outflows is an impure locus; how can it be said to be pure?
Answer: Because it is the opposite of the impurity of the afflictions (*kleśa*), that partial purity can lead to the ultimate purity (*paramārtha-śuddhi*) of the Path. Question:
What is called purity?
The answer is:
the purity of body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the sublime conduct of body and speech of one beyond training, is called purity of body and speech.
That which is called the purity of mind (*manoviśuddhi*) is the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*); that mind of one beyond training is termed the purity of mind.

It attains the mark of a Sage (*mauneya*), is free from the speech of afflictions, severs the braided hair of the three realms, and shaves off the topknot of afflictions based upon the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because the body possesses activity and the mind is not tranquil, it is therefore not called a *muni*.
A *muni* signifies tranquility (*śānti*).
This is taught in order to sever [attachment to] bathing, purification with water, and so forth; for this reason, it is called "purity."
In order to bring an end to [misunderstanding of] the Muni’s teaching, he speaks of the *muni* (sage) of body, speech, and mind.
Having already explained the distinctions among the combinations of karma, the distinctions among the fruits of karma shall now be explained.
Wholesome and unwholesome karma—both are said to have two fruits;
wholesome karma may also have three fruits, while the remainder should be known to have one fruit.

Regarding the statement that both wholesome and unwholesome karma are said to have two fruits: wholesome karma has two kinds of fruits; among those, contaminated wholesome karma has the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) and the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) consists of the wholesome factors of one's own category (*sabhāga*) in subsequent births within the same realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
The retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
For untainted (*anāsrava*) karma that abandons afflictions, there are both the concordant fruit and the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*).

The fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*) refers to the subsequent arising of the noble path following the prior arising of the noble path, wherein all [qualities] increase in similarity without diminishing.
The fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) refers to the severance of all afflictions by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Those unwholesome karmas also have two fruits: the fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Wholesome [karma] may, in some cases, result in three fruits; if it is impure wholesome karma that abandons afflictions, it possesses three fruits.

Regarding the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*), the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*), and the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), these are as in the worldly path that severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

As for the remaining one fruit that should be known: it refers to neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma and other untainted (*anāsrava*) karmas that do not sever the fetters; they possess one fruit, namely, the fruit of reliance.
Question: Those bodily and vocal actions arise from the four great elements, which have the nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Which among these are "actions"?
What are the four great elements that constitute it?
The answer is:
whichever great elements exist in their own realm serve as the basis for bodily and vocal karma.
The untainted [factors] are acquired according to one's capacity; these, in turn, depend upon that capacity.

If there are great bodily and vocal karmas within one’s own stage that serve as their basis—such as the bodily and vocal karmas of the desire realm—they are produced solely by the four great elements of the desire realm; the same applies to those of the form realm.

Regarding the statement that "the untainted [karma] is obtained according to one's power and still relies upon that power": the untainted bodily and vocal karma is obtained according to one's power and still relies upon that specific stage; thus are the four great elements produced.

If the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one should know that it still relies upon the desire realm; likewise, the untainted bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) therein should be understood in this way.

Similarly, when [the untainted path] arises in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one should know that it relies upon that specific level (*bhūmi*) and is produced by the four great elements of that level.

Question: If one is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), having abandoned the precepts of training (śaikṣa-śīla) and attained the precepts of no-more-training (aśaikṣa-śīla), upon what basis does that person abandon the precepts,
and upon what basis do they attain the precepts?
Answer: It arises depending on that particular stage and ceases depending on that particular stage.

One completely relinquishes the past precepts dependent on that stage as well as the future precepts dependent on the five stages, and subsequently acquires the future precepts dependent on the five stages.
The five stages refer to the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Question: As the World-Honored One has spoken of the three obstacles, what are their characteristics?
The answer is:
Uninterrupted and irremediable karma, which extensively gives rise to all afflictions and leads to the experience of retribution in the evil realms— this should be known as an obstacle.
There are three kinds of hindrances, namely: the hindrance of karma, the hindrance of afflictions, and the hindrance of retribution.
Because they obstruct the noble path and the means to the noble path, they are called "hindrances."

As for karmic obstructions, they consist of the five deeds of immediate retribution: namely, killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Sangha, and maliciously drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
Having committed these deeds, one will certainly be reborn next in the Avīci Hell; therefore, it is called "Avīci" (Uninterrupted).
Because they have abandoned and turned their backs on the debt of gratitude owed to their mother and father, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The remaining three types [of obstacles] arise from destroying the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it refers to persistent afflictions and intense afflictions.
Persistent afflictions are those that frequently manifest.
The "afflictions that are beneficial" are the predominant afflictions.
It is the manifest afflictions that are termed "obstructions," not those that are merely possessed [as latencies]. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings equally accomplish various afflictions.
Regarding the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), it refers to the retribution according to where one dwells;
it is not a vessel for the Noble Path because the retribution is characterized by evil.
Question: What is that? Answer:
Because all evil realms, the northern continent of Uttarakuru, and the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are exclusively the stages of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Question:
Among these three types of karma, which is the most grievous?
The answer is:
One should know that lying which causes a schism in the Sangha is an extreme transgression;
it is the most significant fruit among unwholesome deeds, even when compared to the volitional formations of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

Regarding the statement that "one should know that lying to cause a schism in the Saṃgha is an extreme transgression": among all karmic actions, lying to cause a schism in the Saṃgha is the most grievous. Such a person shall dwell in the Avīci Hell for one kalpa, with thirteen masses of fire surrounding their body.

Why is this? Because they perceive what is Dharma as non-Dharma and what is non-Dharma as Dharma; furthermore, by destroying the perception of the Dharma and causing a schism in the Saṃgha that gives rise to a heterodox path, they destroy the Wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, this karma is the most extremely evil among all karmas.
There are two types of schism in the Saṃgha: namely, the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) and the schism of the ritual action (*karmabhedaka*).
Regarding the schism of ritual action: within the same boundary (*sīmā*), performing the *poṣadha* and other ritual actions in separate locations.
Question: Which wholesome karma yields the greatest fruit? Answer:
Among all wholesome volitions, that of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) yields the greatest fruit.

The volition associated with the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the Peak of Existence obtains the greatest fruit among all wholesome states, because it leads to an ultimate quiescence lasting for eighty thousand eons.
Due to the causal conditions of its maturation, the volition associated with the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is said to have a "great fruit.
Furthermore, all volitions associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) have great fruits, because they result in the ultimate exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Chapter Four: On the Proclivities (Anuśaya). Regarding the cycle of existence through the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions, the nature of karma has already been explained in detail.
It is by the power of those karmas and afflictions that one undergoes various births; it does not occur apart from afflictions.
Therefore, wishing to analyze the afflictions, the Teacher spoke thus:
"All existence has a root; karma is its companion that gives rise to a hundred sufferings.
The ninety-eight types of latent proclivities—these the Muni taught as objects for reflection."
"All that exists" refers to existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These three types of existence have the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as their root.
Why is this? This [karma] acts as a companion to karma, capable of producing various sufferings such as those of rebirth.

That karma brings about existence through the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*); its power does not exist apart from the afflictions. Therefore, those who seek liberation should understand this; having understood it, they should distance themselves from it.
Why is this? Just as one who does not recognize an enemy will be harmed by them, so it is in the Sūtras where the Buddha taught that there are seven kinds of *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).

When these are distinguished according to their realms (*dhātu*) and types (*prakāra*), they become ninety-eight *anuśayas*. Specifically, the *anuśaya* of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*), when distinguished by realm, is threefold; when distinguished by type, it is fivefold; and when distinguished by both realm and type, it is fifteenfold.
The underlying tendencies of pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise.
The underlying tendency of aversion (*pratigha*) is differentiated by realm into one and by type into five.
The underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*) is differentiated by realm into three, by type into four, and by both realm and type into twelve.
The fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) are divided into three by way of their objects (*viṣaya*) and four by way of their types (*prakāra*).
They are divided into five by way of their modes of activity (*ākāra*), and twelve by way of both their modes of activity and types.

The two views—the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)—are of one type because they are both abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the path, and thus constitutes two types.
False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) constitute four types.

Thus, there are twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); when distinguished by realm, mode of activity, and category, they become thirty-six underlying tendencies; therefore, there are ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
Question: How is this known? Answer:
Regarding all categories of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), one should know that they are established in two divisions:
namely, those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
From those abandoned by the path of seeing up to those abandoned by the path of cultivation, there are only these various proclivities; there are no others besides them.
"Seeing" (*darśana*) means "to view. Because those [defilements] are severed by seeing, they are called "abandoned by the path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
This statement conveys the meaning of being destroyed by "patience" (*kṣānti*).
"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) has the meaning of repeated practice; because they are abandoned through cultivation, they are called "abandoned by the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).
This explains the meaning of what is abandoned by the path of seeing the nature [of reality].
There are twenty-eight afflictions; one should know that they obstruct the vision of suffering.
When one sees suffering, they are severed and exhausted without remainder.

Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) because they obstruct the vision of suffering; this will be explained hereafter.
Nineteen [factors] are abandoned through the vision of the origin; one should know that it is the same for cessation.
Three more are abandoned through the path of vision; ten are said to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Regarding "nineteen are abandoned through the vision of the origin": because nineteen underlying tendencies (anuśaya) obstruct the vision of the origin, they are abandoned through the vision of the origin.
"One should know that the same applies to cessation" means one should know that seeing cessation also abandons nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"Increasing three for those abandoned by the path of vision" means twenty-two underlying tendencies are abandoned by the path of vision.

Regarding the statement that ten [defilements] are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one should know that these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are to be severed by the path of cultivation.
Having already explained the distinctions among the types of underlying tendencies, the distinctions among their realms (*dhātu*) shall now be explained.
Regarding the first category of afflictions, one should know that there are ten in the desire realm;
in each of the [next] two, there are seven respectively; eight types are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

As for "regarding the first category of afflictions, one should know that there are ten in the desire realm": as previously stated, among the categories of afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are bound within the desire realm. These are: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the statement that "there are seven in each of the two [realms]": as previously explained, the types of afflictions abandoned through the vision of origin and cessation each consist of seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), which likewise belong to the desire realm.

It should be understood that among these ten, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), there are seven.

Regarding the eight types abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), these consist of the aforementioned seven belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) with the addition of the clinging to precepts and rituals.
One should know that in the desire realm, four [defilements] are abandoned through the path of cultivation;
as for the remaining two higher realms, one should know they are likewise obtainable.

Regarding "one should know that in the desire realm, four are abandoned through the path of cultivation": this refers to greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance—such are the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm, which one should know.
Regarding "the remaining [factors] of the two higher realms," this refers to the remaining sixty-two proclivities (*anuśaya*) that pertain to the form and formless realms.
As for "it should be known that they are likewise obtainable," this means that these thirty-one proclivities pertain to the form realm.
Thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya) belong to the formless realm; among the thirty-six, five—the latent disposition of anger—are excluded.
Having already explained the number and the distinctions of the realms of the latent dispositions, their intrinsic nature shall now be explained.
What are called the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, false views,
and the two types of grasping— these should be known as the five afflictions of view.
These five afflictions are all of the nature of view.
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) refers to grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging; this is called the view of a self-body.
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) refers to being attached to the notions of annihilationism or eternalism regarding those [aggregates]; this is called the view of extremes.
Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) refers to the denial of the Four Noble Truths while firmly adhering to such a misconception; this is called wrong view.

Adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to the false attachment to things such as Īśvara, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the *puruṣa*, or the "intermediate knowledge" (*antarā-jñāna*)—which are not actually causes for liberation from suffering—as being the cause thereof, thereby grasping at such rules and rituals. Here, by excluding the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is termed "adherence to rules. Thus, it is called adherence to rules and rituals.

Regarding the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): it consists of grasping at contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as being supreme, thereby clinging to [wrong] views and so forth. This is called "clinging to views" because it excludes other types of clinging.
Since its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is specifically designated as a "view."
These five views encompass all views.
Because this single false view involves wrong attachment and manifests through different modes of activity, it is said to be of five kinds.
Greed, doubt, and hatred, as well as pride and ignorance, are not views.
As they evolve through the differentiation of their objective spheres (*viṣaya*), they are said to have various names.
Regarding "lust, doubt, hatred, pride, and ignorance that are not views": as for lust (*rāga*), it is the craving, longing, and attachment toward existence; this is called lust.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) refers to calculating the true meaning of the truths as being real, or slandering that true meaning, or hesitating regarding it; this is called doubt.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) refers to when one is oppressed by another and, unable to tolerate it, gives rise to malicious intent, causing extreme affliction and destruction toward sentient beings, and giving rise to a mind that harms them inappropriately; this is called hatred.
Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind through comparing oneself with others; this is called pride.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the lack of knowledge regarding the characteristics of the truths and the impure; this is called ignorance.
Because these five afflictions are not of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are not referred to as "views" (*dṛṣṭi*).

Thus, although all these afflictions arise with various distinctions in their objects and are spoken of by various names, these ten afflictions are established under various names because they arise according to the distinctions among their objects.

Among these, that which turns toward [the object] by taking suffering as its condition is said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; the same applies to those abandoned through the vision of origin, and so forth.
[The afflictions] do not operate with respect to all [objects]; they turn toward two [of the three] views, excluding the view of suffering.
Regarding the path, two views are excluded; furthermore, hatred does not operate in the higher realms.

Regarding "inferior suffering in all": the suffering within the desire realm is termed inferior suffering; all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) therein are contrary to the perception of suffering.
Question: In what way are they contrary?
The answer is:

The world is unable to investigate; they do not know the mass of suffering as it truly is. When they hear it said that the aggregates are suffering, they feel neither joy nor delight. This failure to investigate is called ignorance.
Due to ignorance, one conceives doubt therein, wondering: "Is this merely the aggregates, or is there a self?
To give rise to such a thought is called doubt.
To speak erroneously due to doubt, or to slander by claiming that there are no aggregates (*skandha*) because of past habituation, is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To reckon that there is a self (*ātman*) is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Because one perceives that [the aggregates] are similar, continuous, and uninterrupted, the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) arises.
Seeing that the continuity of cause and effect is destroyed and ceases, one gives rise to the view of annihilation due to delusion.
Clinging to both annihilation and permanence is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
To grasp at this view as being pure is called the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
To regard these views and so forth as supreme is called the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To cherish one's own views is called greed (*lobha*).
To feel resentment toward the views of others is called hatred (*dveṣa*).
To exalt oneself by means of this is called pride (*māna*).
In this sequence, these ten afflictions are contrary to suffering (*duḥkha*). Regarding the phrase "excluding three views and two [types of] turning":

with the exception of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remaining seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) turn toward both origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
His lack of knowledge regarding the cause of suffering is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of delusion, doubt arises; this doubting as to whether the cause of suffering exists or does not exist is called doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Due to doubt, one propounds false teachings; or, due to former habits, one slanders the existence of causes for suffering—this is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To grasp at that [wrong view] as superior is called the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Thus, not knowing the truth of cessation—that is, nirvāṇa—is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of this delusion, one is confused as to whether nirvāṇa exists or does not exist;
this is called doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding "the Path excludes two views": the Path excludes the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); the remaining eight types [of afflictions] operate therein.
Lack of faith and acceptance toward that Path is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
All else is as previously explained.

Regarding the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): it is the belief that among these various views, such as the "cow-precepts" and so forth, they constitute purification. Question:
Why do the view of a self and the other [afflictions] not arise with respect to the truths of origin, cessation, and the path?
The answer is:
the view of a self operates within the sphere of the fruit, revolving around the notions of "I" and "mine."

There is no one who holds such a view as to conceive of a self within this cause of suffering, its cessation, and the path; therefore, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) operates within the context of suffering, and thus when the reality of suffering is seen, it is entirely severed without remainder.
Extreme views arise from the view of a self; therefore, they have suffering as their condition.
If one eliminates the view of a self through insight, then by means of that [insight], the extreme views for which it was the condition are also eliminated. Question:

If one who clings to precepts and observances lacks faith in causes and reckons the Lord (*īśvara*) as the cause of the path, how can such a person abandon [defilements] through the vision of suffering?
The answer is:

Such a person is deluded regarding the fruit; they conceive of the aggregates (*skandha*) by means of names such as the "Lord" and so forth, and they constantly discriminate, forming the notion that the Lord and others act as causes. At that time, they are able to observe the Truth of Suffering through modes such as impermanence (*anitya*).
Since the conceptualization of causes such as the "Lord of Calculation" (Īśvara) and so forth is immediately severed, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, because one does not believe in the Path, taking what is not the Path to be the Path, it is abandoned through the vision of the Path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*); however, since the true Path is seen, this [conceptualization] no longer exists within cessation (*nirodha*).
Why is this? Because such [afflictions] do not exist within the path of cessation.
Regarding those who do not engage in anger in the higher realms: in the form and formless realms, with the exception of anger, the rest are as explained for the desire realm.
Why is this? Because they lack the characteristic of harm, possess wholesome desire, are by nature tranquil, and have a moistened mind; therefore, they are without hatred.
The intrinsic natures and distinctions of the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) have already been explained; their distinctions in terms of objects (*ālambana*) shall now be discussed.
Pervasive throughout suffering and its cause, Doubt, [wrong] views, and ignorance— These constitute all categories of latent proclivities, Which are said to reside within a single stage (*bhūmi*).

Among the categories abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there are doubt (*vicikitsā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and their associated ignorance (*sānuśaya-avidyā*), as well as non-associated ignorance (*asāmānya-avidyā*).

These eleven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) should be understood as pervasive within their respective realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*). Within their own stage, they act as conditions for all five categories; they condition those above them, but do not condition those below them.
Why is this? Because their nature is free from desire, the lower does not cause the higher to act. Why is this?
Because it is not within their objective range, it is said that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) operate within their own stage. Question:
What is the meaning of "pervasive" (sarvatraga)?
Answer: It is called the meaning of "pervasive of all" because it takes as its object the meaning of all contaminated things (*sāsrava*).
Since that [object] has arisen from the very beginning within all sentient beings and all contaminated things, it is called the meaning of "pervasive of all."
There is not a single contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharma that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has not originally grasped as "I" or "mine.

Question: For what reason is it said that among the categories abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there are universal factors (*sarvatraga*), but not in those of cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*)?

Answer: Because they take all contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects as their conditions and because they share a single mental orientation, all firmly established contaminated matters are subsumed under the Truths of Suffering and Origination.

As for the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, some take contaminated objects as their conditions and some take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects as their conditions; because they do not share a single mental orientation, they are neither firmly established nor do they take all objects as their conditions.
Question: For what reason are greed, hatred, pride, and so forth not universal? Answer:
Because these are specific latent dispositions (*svalakṣaṇānuśaya*), they arise even with respect to a small portion of a single sentient being.
The universal latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) are not like this, for those that are universal take all realms (*dhātu*) and all stages (*bhūmi*) as their objects.

Through the mental application (*manasikāra*) of greed and so forth, one gives rise to the seeking of sensual desire; that which is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*) functions only toward the manifest misconduct of others, like a flowing river.
Having already explained the all-pervasives of one’s own realm and level (*svadhātu-bhūmi*), those that are all-pervasive across other realms and levels shall now be explained.
The first afflictions are of five kinds; four are said to be the foremost, which operate upon superior objects, as taught by the Omniscient One.

Among the eleven previously mentioned universal [afflictions], with the exception of the two views of self-identity and extremes, the remaining nine afflictions are said to be universal across other realms and stages.
Among those [defilements] of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering: wrong view denies the fruit of suffering in the form and formless realms;
grasping at views takes them to be superior;
and grasping at precepts and observances takes what is not the cause of suffering to be the cause of suffering.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) therein is hesitation; ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion.

Likewise, the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm slanders the cause of the aggregates (*skandha*) of the form and formless realms; the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) regards the causal entity as superior; and doubt regarding the causal entity is hesitation, while ignorance is delusion.
In this way, wrong view within the form realm denies the fruit of suffering in the formless realm; this should be explained in detail.

The same applies to the stages (*bhūmi*): wrong view in the stage of the first dhyāna denies the suffering of the second dhyāna, and so on in detail, up to the sphere of nothingness denying the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are no other universals (sarvatraga) belonging to other realms. Why?
Because there are no higher realms above it.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has no universal [defilements] pertaining to other stages, because there are no higher stages above it.
Question: Why are the two views—view of self and view of extremes—not universal [defilements] pertaining to other realms or stages?
Answer: It does not arise from a different realm or level.
It is illogical for the notion of "self" and "what belongs to self" to arise with respect to the aggregates (skandhas) of a different realm or level.
There is no activity of a dualistic body, for this is not perceived by direct observation.
Since that [body] lacks a self, there is no logical basis for the notion of "mine.
As for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it consists of reckoning one's own aggregates as either annihilated or eternal.
Wrong view and doubt, along with innate and independent ignorance, are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path; one should know that these have the untainted as their object.

The wrong view abandoned through the vision of cessation slanders the Truth of Cessation; doubt is doubt regarding the Truth of Cessation. The ignorance associated with those two, as well as independent ignorance—ignorance which does not perceive the characteristics [of the object] but functions toward the state of cessation—these three afflictions have the Truth of Cessation as their object; therefore, they have the untainted as their object.
It is the same regarding the paths as well.
Thus, within the three realms, there are eighteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) that definitely have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. Question:
Why are the afflictions such as craving (*rāga*), which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), not conditioned by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
The answer is:
if they were conditioned by the outflow-free, one would not perceive the faults of craving; therefore, the latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) is not conditioned by the outflow-free.
If one seeks the path for the cessation of greed, this is a wholesome desire for the Dharma, not the latent tendency of greed.
It is not hatred, because the perception of disparagement does not arise and its intrinsic nature is that of gentleness.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is not something to be proud of.
Being pure and supreme, it is the path to *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is free from the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Commentary by the Venerable Upaśānta on the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
In the second part of the *Anuśaya-varga* of the six-fascicle compilation, there is a separate translation which asks:
"What are those *anuśayas*?
In what places do they function?"
Of all types in the desire realm, the pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) bind by way of their objects within their own stage; it is the same for the higher stages.
Regarding "of all types in the desire realm, the pervasive latent tendencies bind by way of their objects within their own stage": this refers to the pervasive latent tendencies of the desire realm.
Just as it is for all types [of fetters] in the desire realm, so it is for those in the higher realms; likewise for the form and formless realms within their own respective levels.

As for the remaining fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*), one should know that they act as conditions and proclivities within their own category and upon their own level, according to the "All Shared Basis" chapter.

Regarding the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*), one should know that those which function as proclivities by taking their own seeds and their own levels as objects are not universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*). They are proclivities that are bound by taking as their objects only those phenomena within their own category and their own level; such is their respective sphere.

Regarding the category of "all shared dependencies": all pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*) as well as non-pervasive proclivities act as proclivities through association within the associated dharmas of their own kind and their own category.

If they are the objects of the untainted (*anāsrava*), or if they are afflictions (*kleśa*) that take other stages as their object, and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with them, [they are not latent tendencies by way of the object], because they are liberated from the object.

Regarding those which are the objects of the untainted, or those afflictions that take other stages as their object, and the latent tendencies associated with them: if a latent tendency takes the untainted as its object or takes another realm or stage as its object, it is not a latent tendency by way of the object (*ālambanānuśaya*).
Question: Why is that? Answer:
Because of liberation from the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Since these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are liberated from their objective spheres, the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*). Question:
What is meant by "conditioning without causing [bondage]"?
The answer is:
because there is no place of abiding.
Because that [state] is the antidote to the outflows (anāsrava), it provides no place for them to abide.
It is like a blazing lapis lazuli gem upon which mosquitoes and other such insects delight in ascending, yet are unable to remain.
Just as when a person treads upon hot ground, they cannot keep their feet there because of the sensation of heat, so it is with this:
the dharmas of the higher stages liberate one from the lower stages; therefore, although they take them as objects, they do not cause [affliction].
Question: What are these proclivities (*anuśaya*)?
Are they unwholesome (*akuśala*) or are they indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: The view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, along with their co-arising ignorance, are indeterminate within the realm of desire;
they are likewise so in all [stages] of the form and formless realms.

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) associated with them, these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) within the realm of desire; that is, the two views of self-identity and extremes, along with their associated ignorance in the desire realm, are indeterminate.

Why is this? Because it is not in contradiction with giving, morality, and so forth. The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) are not in contradiction with the practice of giving, morality, and meditation.
Why is this? Because one desires to experience desirable fruits in the future, one performs acts such as giving;
since unwholesome states are contrary to giving and the like, they are therefore indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, all sentient beings constantly engage in this view.
If these afflictions were unwholesome, there would not be a single sentient being in the desire realm who could experience pleasure.
Why is this? Because it constantly practices what is unwholesome.
Furthermore, this view is deluded regarding its own object and does not oppress others; therefore, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is not unwholesome.

The view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi) accords with the departure from desire and is proximate to non-self; it can produce the practice of revulsion toward impermanence, and is therefore not unwholesome.
All other afflictions of the desire realm are unwholesome.

Regarding "all [defilements] of the form and formless realms": all latent tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to the form and formless realms are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta); because they are suppressed by the fourfold and fivefold samādhis, they are unable to produce karmic retribution.
For example, just as a potent incantation subdues a venomous snake so that it cannot cause harm, so too is this case.
Furthermore, regarding that which cannot serve as a cause for retribution: the unwholesome does not produce the experience of suffering as its retribution.
Since there is no feeling of suffering in the higher realms, one cannot experience their fruit within the Desire Realm.
Question: How is it that all afflictions invariably function within their own respective spheres?
"Is it so, or not? He replied, "It is not."
Question: How so? Answer:
One should know that greed, hatred, and pride are either bound by their objects in the past, while all of them are said to be so in the future; as for the rest, they are bound in all three times.

Regarding the statement "one should know that greed, hatred, and pride are either bound by their objects in the past": if greed, hatred, pride, and so forth occurred in the past, it is not the case that all of them were bound in the past with respect to their own respective objects.
Why is this? It is not that one does not see or hear;
it is that greed, hatred, and pride do not arise unless one hears and discriminates regarding an object.
Why is this? Because of the limitation of conditions.
For instance, at times a person may give rise to desire for the eye, but not for other parts of the body.
Why is this? Because they are driven by their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
They do not grasp objects in common with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as greed, as is the case with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and others.

Regarding "all that is said to be future": if, in the future, greed, hatred, pride, and so forth, take as their objects all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three times, then among those, if they belong to the five consciousness-bodies (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), they are necessarily bound to the future if they are destined to arise (*utpatti-dharmin*), and they are bound to all three times if they are not destined to arise (*anutpatti-dharmin*).
Furthermore, the dharmas that arise or do not arise in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*) also take as their object all contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of the three periods of time. Why is this?
Because they take all contaminated dharmas as their object.

Regarding "all other [factors] of the three times": view (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are what are termed "the others," because they are bound by common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
