If these are past or future, they bind all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three times through their objective conditions (*ālambana-bandhana*).
Why is this? Because they are universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Since the underlying tendencies of the present are not fixed, they are not mentioned.
If they exist, those self-characteristic proclivities manifest in the present, thereby binding one in the present and the future.
As for "binding in the future," this refers to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and the non-arising of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).
Regarding the past: if, having arisen therein, it has already ceased, yet the bondage within that state remains uninterrupted;
and if the universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) manifest before one, they bind all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) throughout the three periods of time.
Having already explained the distinctions among the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the world, their sequential progression shall now be explained.
The sequential progression of the afflictions (*kleśa*) should be understood as follows:
they arise from their own level within their own level, and also from higher levels down to lower levels. This is how the sequence should be known.

Regarding "the afflictions successively arise within their own stage from their own stage": this means that all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within a given stage arise as successive conditions for the underlying tendencies of that same stage; each one arises in succession for all of them.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that those of higher stages are also born in succession into lower ones": at the time of death in the Brahma-world stage, one is born successively into the desire realm; when all such defiled minds therein reach the end of life, a defiled intermediate state (*antarābhava*) mind of the desire realm arises in succession.
In this manner, it continues up to birth in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), or birth in such a birth, such as being born in the formless realm and being reborn again in the formless realm.
Question: As the World-Honored One has taught, there are seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), beginning with greed.
How are they differentiated into ninety-eight?
The answer is:
the five kinds of greed in the desire realm are here called the latent tendency of sensual craving (*kāmarāgānuśaya*).
The same applies to the form and formless realms; one should know that these constitute the latent tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*).

Regarding the five types of greed in the desire realm, which are here called the latent tendency of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāgānuśaya*): namely, the fivefold sensual greed abandoned through the path of seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through the path of cultivation—these are called the latent tendency of craving for sense-pleasures, as previously explained.

Regarding the statement, "The same applies to the form and formless realms; one should know that there is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)," this means that there are five types in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and likewise five types within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are explained as the underlying tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*).
Hatred itself is the latent tendency of hatred; its five types are as previously explained.
Pride and ignorance—these fifteen exist within the three realms. Regarding the statement "hatred itself is the latent tendency of hatred;

its five types are as previously explained": in the desire realm, there are five types of hatred, which are designated as the latent tendency of hatred based on their abandonment through the vision of suffering and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the fifteen [factors] consisting of pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) exist within the three realms": in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), pride also has five types, such as those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The same five types also exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These fifteen types of conceit are called the latent tendency of conceit (*mānānuśaya*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise.
As for the thirty-six latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), one should know that they exist within the three realms.
The latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) are twelve; briefly explained, they are of seven types.

Regarding the statement "the thirty-six latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) should be known as belonging to the three realms": the thirty-six latent tendencies of views should be understood such that twelve are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). These are: five abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), two abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), two abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), and three abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*). The same applies to the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that there are twelve latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*): four types are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; the same applies to the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
These twelve types are designated as the latent tendencies of doubt.

Regarding the statement that they are briefly explained as sevenfold: although these natures and categories of the realm are differentiated into ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), the World-Honored One briefly explained them as sevenfold in his sūtras.
Question: What is the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: That which has a subtle meaning is the meaning of "proclivity" (anuśaya).
Proclivities function subtly; those that are coarse are called "entanglements" (paryavasthāna).
The meaning of "constantly following and entering" is called a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), like sesame seeds mixed with a paste.
The meaning of "clinging" is called a latent tendency, just as a small child clings to its nursemaid.

The meaning of "continuity" is called a latent tendency, like the poison of a rat, like a quartan fever, like a debt that compounds daily, like the black color of iron that does not leave it, or like the gradual accumulation of recitation and study.
Such afflictions, the Blessed One has described as yokes, floods, clingings, outflows, and bonds.
Question: For what reason?
The answer is:

Because of the meanings of affliction (*ogha*), flow (*srotas*), grasping (*upādāna*), and outflow (*āsrava*), as well as bondage (*bandhana*), it is said: "afflictions, flows, graspings, outflows, and bondages."

The meaning of being bound by suffering is explained as "affliction" (*āsrava*); this is of four kinds, namely: the affliction of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the affliction of existence (*bhavāsrava*), the affliction of views (*dṛṣṭyāsrava*), and the affliction of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).

Because they grasp at birth and the requisites for birth, they are called "grasping" (*upādāna*); these are also of four kinds, namely: grasping at desire (*kāmopādāna*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), and so forth.
They are called "flows" (*āsava*) because they carry sentient beings away; there are also four kinds, as explained in the section on "Calamities.

The meaning of "flowing out" is the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*). Within all births, there are three types of outflows: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).
It is called "bond" (bandhana) because it has the sense of being able to bind the world. Question:
What are the fetters (saṃyojana)?
The answer is:

There are nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely: the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
The distinctions in the names of the afflictions have already been explained; their association with the faculties shall now be discussed.
All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the three realms are entirely associated with the faculties.
According to the faculties belonging to each respective stage, these associations extend up to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that "all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) within the three realms are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)," this means that all afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the three realms are entirely associated with the faculty of equanimity. Why is this?

Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is associated with the faculty of equanimity; it accords with all afflictions and accords with specific afflictions, and ultimately, all afflictions come to rest in a state of neutrality.

Regarding the association of the faculties (*indriya*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with each respective level up to the realm of form (*rūpabhava*): for example, in the Brahma-world there are the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and the latent dispositions therein are associated with these.
Just as the Ābhāsvara Heaven possesses the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of that stage are associated with the faculty of joy.
Furthermore, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven also possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and the latent dispositions therein are associated with the faculty of pleasure.
Wrong view and ignorance, as well as pleasure and pain within the desire realm;
hatred and doubt are exclusively suffering, while the remainder are said to be exclusively pleasure.

Regarding "wrong view and ignorance, as well as pleasure and pain within the desire realm": wrong view in the desire realm is associated with both the faculty of suffering and the faculty of pleasure; when one who holds wrong views performs unwholesome karma, they feel joy, and when they perform wholesome karma, they feel grief. Ignorance, however, is associated with all faculties.

Regarding the statement that hatred (*pratigha*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are associated solely with suffering: because the latent tendency of doubt in the desire realm is indeterminate, it is associated with the faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*) due to its lack of joy.
Because hatred operates toward disagreeable objects, it is associated with both the faculty of physical pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of mental dissatisfaction.

Regarding those that are exclusively associated with pleasure: the remaining afflictions of the desire realm are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). With the exception of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the remaining views, greed, pride, and so forth, function in association with joy.

It is said that they perfume two kinds of bodies; those abandoned through seeing belong only to the mental stage, while the afflictions of the desire realm are said to be associated with the faculties.
Regarding the phrase "it perfumes two kinds of bodies," the afflictions abandoned through cultivation are called "perfuming."
These are associated with bodily feeling and mental feeling; excluding pride, they belong exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).

Among them, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) are said to be bodily feelings, while the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are said to be mental feelings.

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) consists of two types of feeling (*vedanā*): all bodily feelings (*kāyikī vedanā*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while mental feelings (*caitasikī vedanā*) are abandoned in two ways.

As for those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) being restricted to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), this is because the afflictions abandoned through seeing are associated with the mental faculty and the various faculties of mental feeling, and all afflictions abandoned through seeing reside in the mental level.

Regarding the statement that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are associated with the faculties (*indriya*), these necessarily belong to the desire realm; such is the nature of the phenomena of affliction.
For the higher realms as well, their association with the faculties is likewise according to the respective stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*), within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) it is associated exclusively with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
That doubt, being a wholesome mental state that assists the path, is associated with joy.
Having explained the afflictions (*kleśa*), the arising of afflictions shall now be discussed.
Lack of shame and lack of dread, sleep and remorse, stinginess and envy, restlessness and drowsiness—these are the higher fetters of affliction; therefore they are called "arising afflictions.
The messengers are also said to be afflictions.

That which is predominant is the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*); because these eight factors arise therein, they are called "arising of afflictions" and are also termed "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*).

Among them, the three—torpor (*styāna*), sleep (*middha*), and lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*)—arise based on delusion (*moha*); the three—restlessness (*auddhatya*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and lack of dread (*āhrīkya*)—arise based on greed (*lobha*); regret (*kaukṛtya*) arises based on doubt (*vicikitsā*); and envy (*īrṣyā*) arises based on hatred (*dveṣa*).
To commit evil oneself without feeling shame is called *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect).
To disregard others and feel no remorse is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of decorum).
When one sleeps, it renders the mind incapable; because of this attachment to sleep, the five faculties cannot function and the mind lacks mastery.
To give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding agreeable and disagreeable objects, such that the mind is not tranquil, is called *auddhatya* (restlessness).
To have the thought that one has done what should not be done or failed to do what should be done, resulting in subsequent regret and mental fever, is called *kaukṛtya* (remorse).
To feel displeasure in one's heart upon seeing the assets of others is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
To be stingy regarding the Dharma, wealth, or merit—this parsimonious mind that is the opposite of giving—is called avarice (*mātsarya*).
One should know that among all the companions of the afflictions, sleep and restlessness, as well as lack of shame and lack of dread, are invariably associated with the unwholesome.

Regarding the statement "one should know that among all the companions of the afflictions, sleep and restlessness [are associated with them]": these two types of arisen afflictions are associated with all afflictions.
Why is this? Because it pervades the three realms and because all afflictions are not stilled, one should know this as restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Because afflictions manifest and there is no capacity for the wholesome, one should know this as torpor (*styāna*).

Regarding the statement that "lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) are necessarily associated with the unwholesome": these two give rise to afflictions and are associated with unwholesome latent tendencies (anuśaya), because in the desire realm they are invariably unwholesome.
"Remorse exists in the mental [consciousness] and is said to be suffering; it is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
Sleep exists only in the desire realm and the mental [consciousness]; the others are each established individually.

Regarding "remorse exists in the mental [consciousness] and is said to be suffering": remorse arises in the inferior level of the mental stage; therefore, it is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding the teaching on suffering, one should know that it pertains to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and not to the higher realms.
Question: By whom is it abandoned?
Answer: It is abandoned through the cultivation of the path (bhāvanā-heya).
Since regret pertains to both good and evil conduct, it is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.

Regarding the statement that "sleep exists only in the mental [consciousness] of the desire realm": sleep resides in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and at the time of sleep, it functions in conjunction with all afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is associated with all afflictions of the mental stage within the desire realm.

Regarding "the others are each established independently": "the others" refers to stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*). These function through their own power and are not associated with other afflictions.

In meaning, they exclude ignorance (*avidyā*); they are definitely abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and are associated with the latent tendency of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā-anuśaya*).
Question: With how many groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya) are these proclivities (anuśaya) associated? Answer:
Greed, hatred, and delusion— One should know that they depend on the six consciousnesses;
That is to say, they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the desire realm, and in the higher realms, they correspond to whichever [consciousness] is attained.

Regarding "greed, hatred, and delusion—one should know that they depend on the six consciousnesses; that is to say, they are abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm": this means that in the desire realm, craving (rāga), aversion (pratigha), and ignorance (avidyā) are associated with the six consciousnesses and are abandoned by the path of cultivation.
If they are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they exist only in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

Regarding those belonging to the higher grounds—such as craving and ignorance pertaining to the form and formless realms—they are associated with whichever aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) is obtained in those respective levels.
Just as forty-four groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya) are found in the Brahma-world, therein two latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with four groups of consciousness;
above this level, they are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), because the remaining latent dispositions therein reside solely in the sphere of the mind (manobhūmi).
The analysis of the afflictions has already been completed; the abandonment of that analysis shall now be explained.
The abandonment of all afflictions is taught as being through the wisdom of skillful means;
one should know that such liberation is not attained all at once.

Regarding that which is taught as the wisdom of the skillful means for severing all afflictions: these afflictions are severed all at once within the path of non-obstruction; they are not severed repeatedly.

There are four kinds of abandonment: namely, abandonment through knowledge of the object, abandonment through the abandonment of companions, abandonment through the object itself, and self-purification.

Regarding "abandonment through knowledge of the object," this refers to that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, whether it has its own realm as its object or is objectless (untainted).
"Accompanied by abandonment" refers to that which has objects belonging to other realms.
"Abandonment of objects" refers to those with outflowing objects (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned through the cessation and the path truths.
"Self-purification" refers to that which is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); as each respective [defilement] is abandoned, one's own continuum becomes purified accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "one should know that such liberation is not attained all at once": this attainment of liberation occurs repeatedly according to those [moments].

For example, in the desire realm, the five types of abandonments through seeing are realized at five times, namely, at the time of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), such as the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) for the abandonments through seeing suffering.

In this manner, up to and including the dharma-knowledge of the path that abandons the path of seeing, as well as the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: regarding what was previously abandoned, the fruit of srotāpanna comprises the arising of one acquisition of liberation; the same applies to the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat. The same also applies to the three truths of the form and formless realms.
In this context, "counteractive of its own category" (*svabhāga-pratipakṣa*) is taught.

Regarding those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by means of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) definitively abandon them and realize their cessation.
Since those abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) are abandoned all at once, there is no "counteractive of its own category" in this case.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they are determined by five periods, as previously explained.

As for those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) according to the sequential dharma of the noble ones (*ārya*), these are the specific antidotes for the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; that is to say, they are determined to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

The three periods of the desire realm refer to the stage of ordinary beings, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*; all these constitute the factors to be abandoned by their respective specific antidotes (*svabhāga-pratipakṣa*).
Within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the two types of the form realm—namely, the "homogeneous" (*svabhāga*) and the "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*)—are not mentioned.

Regarding the homogeneous and antidote aspects of the fruit of arhatship: the former refers to all [levels] within the form realm that are free from desire, while the latter refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding all the factors abandoned through the fruit of arhatship, the realization of their cessation has already been explained; now, the knowledge of abandonment shall be discussed.
The Buddha taught four knowledges of abandonment concerning liberation within the desire realm.
Regarding the liberations of the form and formless realms, one should know that there are five types of abandonment-knowledge (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Because one attains untainted liberation through the exhaustion of causes and the abandonment [of defilements], one establishes abandonment-knowledge upon crossing over the realms.
Why is this? Because liberation without remainder is designated by the name "abandonment.

There are nine types of such abandonment; among them, that which abandons the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin attains liberation without remainder.

Why is this? Because it is abandoned by opening up the universal cause, this first [category] is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahāṇa*). The second is abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-prahāṇa*);

the third is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahāṇa*); and the fourth is the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-vibhāga*). The same applies to the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
The three [fetters] abandoned through seeing are as previously explained.
The fourth is abandoned through the path of cultivation in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), because this involves the complete separation from desire for form.
The fifth is abandoned through the path of cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because this involves the exhaustion of all fetters.

Regarding this analytical knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), there are two types: namely, the attainment of the fruit of *anāgāmin* and the fruit of *arhat*. This is because one crosses over the realms and attains these fruits at these two stages.
Question: Are the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*), or dissociated from it (*citta-viprayukta*)? The Vibhajyavādins say:
Because it is non-associated with the mind, doubt arises.
The answer is:
it is definitely associated.
Why is this? Because it creates afflictions for the mind and obstructs the characteristics of pure dharmas;
yet, since all various sublime virtues can still be attained, it is not the case that they are incompatible.
Regarding that which causes affliction to the mind: if it were definitively dissociated from the mind, it should not cause affliction to the mind, just as external objects such as form do not.
However, they act as afflictions for the mind; as it is said that "lust defiles the mind," by this statement one should know that they are associated [with the mind].
As for "obstruction": if these were not associated with the mind, they would not obstruct when wholesome wisdom arises, and they should be like space, which does not create obstruction.
Since they now act as obstacles, we know they are associated [with the mind].

As for their opposition to purity: if the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) were not associated with the mind, they would not be in opposition to the wholesome; and since they would not be in opposition, they would not be faults.
However, because they constitute a fault, one must know that they are contradictory.
If they are contradictory, then one knows they are associated.

Regarding the fact that various excellent virtues can be attained: if you claim that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are contradictory to virtue and are not associated with the mind, then as these dispositions would constantly continue within it, virtue should be unable to arise.
Since it is observed that wholesome dharmas can arise [from them], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not dissociated; rather, they are associated.
Chapter Five: The Noble Ones (*Ārya*). Having already explained the sequence of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), the sequence of non-transmigration shall now be explained.
The noble sages abandon such things as the various terrors and ferocities of affliction;
through diligence, skillful means, and wisdom, they listen well to those skillful means.
As for "noble sages" (ārya), they are so named because they are worthy of receiving offerings among gods and humans.
"Abandoning" (prahāṇa) means to relinquish.
"Such as" (tadyathā) means, for instance, by way of skillful means (upāya) or in this manner.
"This" (idam) refers to the sequential explanation intended to clarify its characteristics.
Regarding "afflictions" (*kleśa*): they are called afflictions because they cause sentient beings to experience continuous vexation and fatigue.
Regarding "the source of all terrors and wildness": this refers to the meaning of being the cause of all suffering and distress.
"Right effort" (samyag-vyāyāma) means effort in accordance with the Dharma.
"Skillful means wisdom" (upāya-jñāna) refers to the meaning of the wisdom that governs the timing of cultivation, arousal, and relinquishment, namely *śamatha*.
"Skillful means" (upāya) refers to the meaning of those very skillful means.
"One who listens well" means listening with a sincere mind; it refers to the meaning held by the wisdom of listening.
"Expedient means" refers to individuals ranging from those at the stage of a beginner to those at the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the practitioner who employs the skillful means of the precepts and so forth, the initial practice shall now be explained:
At first, upon a single part of the body, the practitioner binds his own mind;
binding it firmly to the foundation of consciousness, he acts to slay the enemy of wisdom.
Regarding the practitioner who begins with one part of the body and focuses on their own mind, a question is asked:
"Where does one focus?
The answer is:

Whether at the tip of the nose or between the eyebrows, one practices through the three skillful means of the contemplation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), and the elements and sense bases (*dhātu-āyatana*).
It is taught that the binding of the mind occurs within the parts of one's own body, not upon external phenomena.
Although external conditions exist, he does not speak of them through skillful means.
Question: For what reason does he fix his mind [on this]?
The answer is:
It is bound to the basis of consciousness.
The nature of the mind is restless, turbulent, and unstable, like a startled monkey; this is the meaning of being bound to a single object.
Question: For what reason does one fix [the mind] upon a single object? Answer:
To slay the enemy of wisdom—
this true enemy of wisdom being the afflictions (kleśa)—
one must, for the purpose of severing them, contemplate reality with a one-pointed mind, not with a distracted mind.
Because one sees things as they truly are, one is able to sever the afflictions; for this reason, it is said as follows:
"Through this skillful means regarding the body, one determines its true characteristic;
likewise, one contemplates all sensations, one's own mind, and phenomena in accordance with reality."
Because the mind is focused on a single object, one contemplates the true nature of the body.
The "true nature of the body" refers to that which is non-perverted and whose characteristics accord with reality. Question:
What is the true characteristic of the body?
The answer is:
its specific characteristic and its general characteristic.
Their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) refer to the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the portion of form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are what are called impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Such meanings as these do not disturb the mind.

Within the three skillful means, the practitioner brings them forth according to their inclination; through the sequential practice of these skillful means, they attain certainty regarding the true mark of the body.
When this practitioner contemplates that the color of the subtle atoms disperses and disintegrates moment by moment, the contemplation of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is perfected.

Just as water flows through a furrow, the dharma enters the contemplation of sensation (vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna). Among formless dharmas, sensation is the coarsest; therefore, after contemplating the body, one next contemplates sensation.
When this person contemplates the specific and general characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*), at that time the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) is fulfilled.
Since that sensation depends upon the mind (*citta*), one next contemplates the mind immediately after sensation.

In this stage as well, the application of mindfulness to the mind is fulfilled through the definitive understanding of both specific and general characteristics; at that time, for the purpose of observing the remaining phenomena, one enters the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

As for the remaining phenomena, namely the two aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), one likewise contemplates their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); at that time, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is fulfilled.
Entering into the Dharma through general contemplation, one attains the true characteristic of phenomena:
these four are impermanent, empty, non-self, and not blissful.

Regarding "entering into the Dharma through general contemplation and attaining the true characteristic of phenomena": having entered the remaining foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the practitioner understands their respective limits and cultivates skillful means by taking those foundations as objects of mindfulness.

Regarding all phenomena, one repeatedly cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body through the common characteristic of disintegration, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena through the common characteristic of the body and feelings.
In this way, with the body and mind as objects, there are three and two [foundations of mindfulness] respectively; one should know that such is the foundation of mindfulness of disintegration.
Having repeatedly cultivated these through habitual practice, one subsequently performs a collective contemplation of all four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
It is asked: How so?
Answer: These four are impermanent, empty, non-self, and not pleasure.

One contemplates in their entirety that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have such meanings as impermanence and so forth: they are impermanent because they perish and disintegrate moment by moment; they are empty because they are void and non-existent; they are non-self because they lack sovereignty; and they are not pleasure because the three types of suffering constantly pursue them.
That person, wishing to destroy the afflictions and seeking their primary source, analyzes the truths according to the distinctions of cause and effect as they perceive them in the phenomena.
Within that, there are two kinds of cause and effect:
those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
That which is with outflows consists of the cause of accumulation and the fruit of suffering;
that which is without outflows consists of the cause of the path and the fruit of cessation.

Having thus distinguished the truths, that person first proceeds through the stages of hearing and reflecting upon the specific and general characteristics of the stations of mindfulness, grasping their respective limits and distributing them within the objects of the truths.
At that time, one contemplates the sixteen aspects within the four foundations of mindfulness and the four noble truths, which dismantle the conditions for existence.
From this stage, it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*);
arising from the awakening to phenomena, the sixteen aspects emerge as one observes the four noble truths.

Regarding the statement, "From this point on, it is called 'Heat' (ūṣmagata) because it arises from the awakening to phenomena": when a practitioner contemplates the foundations of mindfulness of common phenomena (sādhāraṇa-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna), the very first thing cultivated thereafter is the foundation of mindfulness of common phenomena established in continuous succession; this is designated as the noble root of merit known as "Heat."
Question: How many modes of activity does that dharma have, and what is its objective sphere? Answer:
One observes the Four Noble Truths through the arising of the sixteen aspects.
The practitioner observes the Four Truths by means of these sixteen aspects; therein, they observe the Truth of Suffering through four aspects:

it is impermanent because that which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, has departed; it is suffering because it is pursued by the three types of suffering; it is empty because it is internally devoid of a person; and it is non-self because it lacks autonomy.

In this way, one also examines the truth of origination through four aspects: it is the cause because it produces similar results; it is origination (*samudaya*) because it can generate the process of transmigration; it is existence (*bhava*) because it can draw forth all of birth and death; and it is condition (*pratyaya*) because it brings together dissimilar phenomena.

One also contemplates the truth of cessation through four aspects: it is "cessation" because it is diametrically opposed to all birth and death; it is "tranquility" because it is free from the fire of all afflictions; it is "sublime" because it is supreme among all phenomena; and it is "renunciation" because it can relinquish birth and death.

One also observes the Truth of the Path through four aspects: it is the "Path" because it leads to the state beyond categories; it is "Right" because it is non-erroneous; it is the "Track" because it is the place trodden by all the Noble Ones; and it is the "Exit" because it transcends birth and death.
Question: What is the meaning of "Heat" (ūṣmagata)? Answer:
Wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge is like two fire-drills rubbed together; it is able to exhaust all modes of existence and give rise to the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Because its characteristic is "warmth," it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Once these dharmas have increased, they give rise to the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*), followed by the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), which depend upon a single moment. Regarding the statement that "once these dharmas have increased, they give rise to the Summits and Patience":

because the practitioner enters into right exertion, they obtain the wholesome factors conducive to the path. By following the various requisites and increasing their power of superior progress, once the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) has been increased and perfected, that person cultivates the application of mindfulness toward all phenomena of suffering; the arising of this superior root of goodness is called the "Summits."
Question: What is the meaning of "summit" (mūrdhan)? Answer:
The roots of goodness are immovable.
When one dwells in this "Summit" stage, because one is free from all faults, one is able to enter into "Patience.
If one does not do so, one will regress and remain at the "Heat" stage.
Just as a person climbing a mountain will fall to the four sides if they do not reach the summit, so it is with the practitioner:
when right application continues and the "summit" has increased, there subsequently arises a root of goodness called "receptivity in accordance with the truths" (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*).

This is the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding all shared dharmas; it excels those two types of dharmas by observing the Four Noble Truths through the sixteen aspects (ṣoḍaśākāra).
Question: What is the meaning of "patience" (kṣānti)?
The answer is:
Because one desires the increase of the contemplations on the four truths, such as impermanence and so forth, it is called "patience" (kṣānti).

Therefore, it is said that *anuloma-kṣānti* removes the superior delusion regarding the four truths; while *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* remove the inferior and middling delusions regarding the four truths, but not the superior.
Once patience (*kṣānti*) has increased, it is followed by the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which lasts for a single moment.

Once patience has increased, all the shared applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) reach their peak; therefore, there arises this most excellent root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) among all mundane virtues.
Because it first opens the gateway to the Noble Path, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Some say it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma because it is the most excellent within the mundane world.

This dharma arises in a single moment; once this practitioner has opened the gate to Nirvana, because it serves as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and those supreme qualities—all these roots of goodness are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Question: You say that the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) serves as the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) for the Noble Path; how then can it have the nature of the five aggregates? Answer:

The mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) share the same sequential condition (samanantara-pratyaya), while matter (rūpa) and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) conform to a single fruit; therefore, there is no fault.
Question: What is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of this "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma)?
Answer: The Truth of Suffering; that is the meaning of taking the Truth of Suffering as its object. Question:
How many practices are there?
The answer is:
four practices.
If the four aspects of the sphere of the Truth of Suffering are as described above, he practices these aspects.
Question: To how many stages (bhūmi) do they belong?
Answer: It arises in six stages; one should know these are the preliminary (anāgāmya), the intermediate (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas. Question:
By how many stages (*bhūmi*) are the remaining factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) subsumed? Answer:
The others likewise depend on six stages; they too belong to six stages, just like the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: For what reason are the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) subsumed within the six stages? Answer:
From that, the Path of Seeing can arise.
That stage possesses the Path of Seeing; wherever there is the Path of Seeing, these [factors] are present there. Why is this?
Because it is an attendant of the path of seeing, it is thus:
from the Supreme Mundane Dharma, there necessarily arises Receptivity;
following Receptivity, Knowledge arises, which is able to awaken to the suffering of the lower realm.

Immediately following the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), patience (*kṣānti*) must necessarily arise; the sequence of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others arises as described in the preceding section on causes, up until the point where they can produce the supreme mundane dharma, and the supreme mundane dharma in turn produces the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.

The antidote to the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm is called the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

Because it is the desire to know the dharmas previously unseen and is characterized by joy, it is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*); this is the first untainted path of non-obstruction (*anāsrava-ānantarya-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that "after patience, knowledge arises": immediately following the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*, the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* arises, which has the nature of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question: What is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of this patience and knowledge?
Answer: It is able to awaken to the suffering of the lower realm.
"Suffering of the lower realm" refers to the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
These two types of conditions have such a meaning:
namely, suffering in the realms of form and formlessness, as well as its origin, cessation, and the path;
the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of these dharmas proceeds from sixteen moments of mind.

Regarding "suffering in the form and formless realms," suffering in the form and formless realms is likewise [comprised of] the patience of arising (*utpāda-kṣānti*), the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The Noble Ones also speak of the patience of subsequent inference regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent inferential knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
The same applies to the origin, cessation, and the path: the origin, cessation, and the path likewise arise in this manner.

There are four distinct meanings: the two types of patience (*kṣānti*) constitute the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*) constitute the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that "this dharma is realized through clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) within sixteen moments of mind": during these sixteen moments of mind, one achieves clear comprehension.
Clear comprehension has the meaning of "seeing" (*darśana*).
These fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the final moment of mind is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
From this point onward is called the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*), extending up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
This is subsequently called the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtādhikāra-bhūmi*).
Briefly stated, there are three stages: the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).
I shall now explain the persons established according to these stages.
The one who practices according to the Dharma (dharmānusārī) is one of keen faculties (tīkṣṇendriya) found among these fifteen;
the one who practices according to faith (śraddhānusārī) is not of keen faculties, and it should be known that he is also included therein.

Regarding "the one who practices according to the Dharma is one of keen faculties found among these fifteen": this refers to those individuals comprised within the fifteen moments of mind belonging to the path of seeing (darśanamārga); if they possess keen faculties, they are called "those who practice according to the Dharma."
Because wisdom follows the practice of the Dharma, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*); this obstructs faith in the teachings of others.

It should be understood that "practice in accordance with faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) is likewise included therein; that is, among these persons of fifteen moments of mind, those of duller wisdom are called "practitioners in accordance with faith," which means they practice by relying on faith in the teachings of others.
When that person’s faith manifests and their wisdom accords with it, they practice the Dharma in a manner contrary to those [wrong views].
Not yet free from the desires of the desire realm, they proceed toward the first fruit;
in the second, six [factors] are abandoned; in the third, nine are abandoned, becoming stainless.

Those who have not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm and are proceeding toward the first fruit—namely, those practitioners following by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those following by dharma (dharmānusārin)—who previously had not abandoned desire and possessed all fetters until reaching the stage of certainty, are called "those proceeding toward the fruit of srotāpanna."

Regarding the second point, the abandonment of the six: the afflictions to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path in the desire realm are divided into nine types, namely: the lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low; the lowest-of-the-middle, the middle-of-the-middle, and the highest-of-the-middle; and the lowest-of-the-high, the middle-of-the-high, and the highest-of-the-high.

When those practitioners by faith and practitioners by dharma, while still on the stage of ordinary beings, have already eradicated the six types of afflictions and subsequently entered the state of certainty, they are at that time said to be heading toward the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin.

Regarding the third, the "ninefold stainless" (navānāsrava): if, after eradicating the nine kinds of afflictions, one enters the state of certainty (*niyāma*), at that time it is said that one is "heading toward" the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is said to be "abiding in the fruit.
One with weak vision is called "liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*); one with pure vision is called "attained to vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

If one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, this is said to be abiding in the fruit. While in the sixteenth moment of mind, that which arises in association with the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) is called abiding in the fruit, whether one possesses sharp faculties or dull faculties.
First, before one has abandoned desire, there is the fruit of srotāpanna;
having abandoned six types of desire, there is the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin;
having abandoned nine types of desire, there is the fruit of anāgāmin.

Regarding those with weak vision who are liberated through faith: if they possess weak faculties, they are called "faith-followers" (śraddhānusārin) while progressing toward the stages; when they abide in the three fruits, they are called "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Regarding those with pure vision who are said to have reached vision: those with sharp faculties abiding in the fruits are called "attainers of vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
As long as the abandonments through the path of cultivation are not yet exhausted, one should know that there will be seven more往返 (return-and-go).
One who has three [further] exhaustions among the various families dwells as a *srotāpanna*.

Regarding "as long as the abandonments through the path of cultivation are not yet exhausted, one should know that there will be seven more return-and-gos": because this person, while abiding in the fruit, has not yet abandoned the abandonments through the path of cultivation, it should be known that they will undergo seven births and deaths.

They undergo seven births among humans and seven births among the gods of the desire realm; including the twenty-eight births of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they all undergo seven births each, and are therefore called "seven-birthers" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*).
As with the *saptaparṇa* tree, so it is with the "one well-versed in the seven points.

Regarding those who have three [types of] destruction among the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioners—whether they abide in the fruit or are ordinary persons—it is said that when the three types among those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm—namely, the superior-superior, the superior-middle, and the superior-inferior—are destroyed, they are called "family-to-family."

Regarding the "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*): because they go from one household to another, coming and going until they enter *nirvāṇa*, they are called "one who goes from family to family.
They come and go among two or three families among humans and two or three families among devas; this is of two types, namely, the human *kulaṃkula* and the celestial *kulaṃkula*.
They are called *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) because of the distinctions in their karma, faculties, and the severance of afflictions.
"Karma" refers to the karma accumulated that results in two or three more existences within the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Faculties" refers to the attainment of the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Those who have severed the afflictions sever three or four types of afflictions.

Those who abide as stream-enterers (srotāpanna)—namely, those who will be reborn seven times at most (saptakṛtvahparama) and those who go from family to family (kulaṃkula)—are said to abide in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala).
Question: For what reason is one called a *srotāpanna*? Answer:

*Srotas* means "stream of the noble path," and *āpanna* means "entered. If a person, through the continuity of their being, first sees the path of cultivation and enters that stream, and furthermore attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, they are therefore called a *srotāpanna*.
Like a daughter in the womb wrapped in swaddling clothes, one is called a "person by way of dharma.

When the six [defilements] are exhausted, one is a Sakṛdāgāmin; when eight or one type of seed is abandoned, one is an Anāgāmin, for the nine grades are all exhausted and one has thus emerged from the mire of desire.

Regarding the "sixth extinction of the once-returner" (ṣaṣṭha-sakṛdāgāmin): if a person has severed the six types of afflictions—namely, the three superior grades and the three middle grades—they are a once-returner.
Passing away from this life, they are reborn in the heavens, and being reborn again among humans, they attain parinirvāṇa; such a person is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).
"Free from eight types of seeds" refers to the meaning of having one remaining birth-seed.
That person has only one more birth remaining, whether as a human or a deva.
There is one type of "one-seed" (ekabījika): namely, the human one-seeder and the deva one-seeder.

Alternatively, the specific distinction of the afflictions is termed "one-seeded" (*ekabījika*); because they have only one remaining existence (*bhava*) that is not yet exhausted, they are called "one-seeded.
Such a person is a candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and it should be understood that this is subsumed within the superior path (*viśeṣamārga*) of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Regarding those who have exhausted all nine grades [of defilements] and are non-returners (*anāgāmin*): if a person has abandoned all nine types of afflictions of the desire realm, they are called an *anāgāmin*.
Because they do not return to be born again in the desire realm, they are called an *anāgāmin*.
Question: For what reason does one not return? Answer:
Because he has already emerged from the mire of desire.
Having emerged from the mire of craving and desire, he therefore does not return again to the desire realm.
Thus, these nine afflictions reside within the eight higher stages.
"That which is abandoned by the two paths has been taught by the World-Honored One.

Thus, regarding the nine afflictions that exist in the eight higher stages, and the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation as previously described, there are nine types of afflictions ranging from the lowest-of-the-low to the highest-of-the-high.
One should know that the eighth stage is likewise: namely, the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), which are abandoned by the path of the pair.

As taught by the World-Honored One, those afflictions of the three realms should be known as being abandoned by the path of unimpeded liberation (*anantarya-vimukti-mārga*). One attains liberation through the abandonment of fetters by the path of non-obstruction; specifically, the lower-of-the-lower path abandons the upper-of-the-upper seeds, continuing in this manner until the upper-of-the-upper path abandons the lower-of-the-lower seeds.
This has been a brief explanation of the one hundred and seventy-eight paths and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). Question:
How is it determined that the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*) abandons the afflictions?
"Is it so, or not? He replied, "It is not."
Question: How so? Answer:
The defiled and the undefiled paths, both are able to transcend the eight stages;
abiding therein, one is said to be a "body-witness," meaning one has attained the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding the statement that both the defiled and the undefiled paths are able to transcend the eight stages: the "defiled" refers to the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), and the "undefiled" refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

Those eight stages are the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments. The mundane and supramundane paths are able to transcend them; among these, it is necessarily the supramundane path that can transcend those [stages] via the mundane path, consisting of both the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
That path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) proceeds in three ways, namely: as suffering (duḥkha), as coarse (audārika), and as an obstacle (āvaraṇa).
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) likewise has three aspects, namely: as superior (praṇīta), as excellent (viśeṣa), and as escape (niḥsaraṇa).
The mundane paths are as previously described, such as the contemplation of impermanence (anitya-saṃjñā) and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "one who dwells therein is called a 'bodily witness' (kāyasākṣin) because they have attained the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)": among those dwelling in the state of training (śaikṣa) within the detachment from the eight stages [of the form realm], if one attains the meditative attainment of cessation, they are termed a "bodily witness."
Because it is a dharma similar to the realization of nirvana through the body, it is called "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
Following the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) necessarily arises;
having produced the thought, "Birth for me is exhausted," the Arhat is free from all outflows (āsrava).

Regarding the statement that the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) is necessarily followed by the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna): the ninth path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) that brings about detachment from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is called the diamond-like samādhi because it is the final mind of a trainee (śaikṣa), which—like a diamond—is incapable of being destroyed; immediately thereafter, the knowledge of exhaustion necessarily arises.

In this case, the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) differs from those two knowledges; it is either the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*).
Just as when that person arises from the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), they produce wisdom that accords with and follows the object of exhaustion (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement "I have exhausted birth," one should know that this refers to birth within the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Why is this so? Because it is the final [state] to be severed.
Regarding the Arhat who is free from all outflows (*āsrava*): when his knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, all outflows are exhausted, and he is thus called an Arhat.
Because he is worthy of receiving offerings among gods and humans, he is named an Arhat.
Question: How many kinds of Arhats are there? Answer:
There are six types of Arhats; five arise from faith. They attain two kinds of knowledge;
one should know them as those who are "timely" and "stainless. Regarding the six types of Arhats:

they are the one of falling nature (*parihāṇadharman*), the one of reflecting nature (*cetayitadharman*), the one of guarding nature (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one of abiding nature (*sthitākampyadharman*), the one of advancing nature (*prativedhanādharman*), and the one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).

Among them, if a person possesses weak wisdom and weak skillful means, and is initially endowed with the factors for retrogression, they will certainly fall back; therefore, they are called "one subject to retrogression" (*parihāṇadharman*).

If a person possesses weak wisdom and weak skillful means, yet constantly feels aversion toward the body and desires its destruction through death, they achieve the state of "one intent on reflection" (*cetana-dharman*).
If one possesses mild wisdom and superior diligence, protecting oneself through the power of diligence, this is called "protecting the Dharma" (dharmarakṣā).
If one possesses middling wisdom and balanced diligence, abiding in this path without advancing or retreating, it is therefore called "abiding in the Dharma" (dharmasthiti).
If one possesses sharp wisdom and extreme refinement, and through diligence is certain to advance to the immovable stage, this is called the "Dharma of Certain Progression.
If one possesses sharp wisdom and broad diligence, attaining the immovable stage at the outset, this is called the "Immovable Dharma."

Regarding the statement, "Five arise from faith; they obtain two kinds of knowledge": among these six types of arhats, the first five were originally followers by way of faith (śraddhānusārin); they possess two kinds of knowledge:
the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).
He may at times regress; therefore, he does not give rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
His knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) lasts for either a single moment, or—if it is followed by the manifestation of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*)—it increases.
If that [liberation] manifests before one, it should be known that the "Stainless One" (vimala) at that time is one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
He observes the country, the time, his companions, the teaching of the Dharma, the robes and food, and so forth, as he advances in the cultivation of wholesome roots.
Because this portion of wholesome roots is not cultivated at all times according to one's desire, it is called "liberation by time" (*samaya-vimukta*).
Those of immovable dharma and sharp faculties are "liberated independent of time" (*asamaya-vimukta*);
they attain the three knowledges and achieve self-liberation.

Regarding those of immovable dharma and sharp faculties who are liberated at any time: if a person possesses exclusively sharp faculties and is of immovable dharma, one should know that they are liberated at any time.
That person, being well-portioned, advances at all times according to their desire without regard for the specific occasion; therefore, they are called one liberated at any time (asamaya-vimukta).

As for those who have attained the three knowledges, they give rise to the three knowledges, namely: the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi).
This is the dharma of non-retrogression; therefore, one gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

For such a person, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) occurs for a single moment, and the knowledge of non-arising occurs either for a single moment or, if it follows in succession, when the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) manifests before them, or when they attain further advancement, then that [knowledge of non-arising] manifests before them.
Regarding "one who has achieved liberation by oneself," such a person achieves a liberation that corresponds to their own [nature].
It should be understood that "one liberated by time" (samaya-vimukta) is one who attains liberation at a specific, determined time.
One who has achieved the "immovable" (akopya) cannot be moved by those afflictions; because it is like a royal seal, it is called "immovable.
It should be known that one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
only one who is doubly liberated (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) achieves the meditative absorption of cessation.

It should be understood that one who is liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is, among the six types of arhats, one who has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation; it should be known that such a person is liberated by wisdom.
One liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) is so named because they attain liberation solely through the power of wisdom.

As for one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), who has accomplished the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti): among the six types of arhats, it should be known that whoever attains the meditative attainment of cessation is one liberated both ways.
By the power of wisdom, one attains liberation from the hindrance of afflictions;
by the power of meditative concentration, one attains liberation from the hindrance to liberation.
For this reason, they are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
The noble individuals mentioned above are, in brief, of two kinds: namely, those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
One trains for the sake of abandoning the afflictions; this is called "training."
One is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) not because one has not severed the afflictions, but because one has completed the training.
Why is there no further training? Because the training has been brought to its conclusion.
Having already distinguished the noble persons, the differentiation of their dharmas shall now be explained.
Whether it be the dharma of one who follows by faith or the dharma of one who follows by dharma,
such paths of seeing the truths are all identical in their single characteristic.

Whether it be the dharma of one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin) or the dharma of one who follows by dharma (dharmānusārin), once they have seen the truths (satyadarśana), they possess the same single characteristic.

Within the path of seeing the truths, there is a distinction between those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma; the latter are designated as "persons" (pudgala) based on their practice of the dharma.
Among those, the enumeration of the faculties is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).
All other dharmas belonging to those in training (śaikṣa) are called by the wise the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya).

Regarding the statement, "Among those, the enumeration of the faculties is called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown': within that which is subsumed under the path of seeing (darśanamārga), the enumeration of the faculties consists of the so-called mind-faculty (manendriya), pleasure-faculty (sukhendriya), joy-faculty (saumanasyendriya), equanimity-faculty (upekṣendriya), and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhādi-pañcendriya); these are termed the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'."
Because one has not yet known what is to be known, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
It should be understood that such a faculty belongs to a person who is comprised within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

As for those other dharmas of the trainee (*śaikṣa*) which the wise call the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), these refer to the various faculties and dharmas from the stage above the path of vision onward, which are designated as the faculty of knowing.
Because one knows what has already been known, it is called the faculty of "having known.
One should understand that such faculties belong to a person who is engaged in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Among these, the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) should be understood as the faculty of "having known."
"One attains the fruit and abandons the preceding path; this meaning should be understood.

Regarding the statement "among these, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) should be known as the faculty of 'having known' (ājñātāvīndriya)": among the dharmas of one beyond training, these very faculties, as enumerated dharmas, are designated by the name "faculty of having known."
Because there is nothing further to be known once it has been known, it is called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
One should understand that such a faculty belongs to a person (*pudgala*) comprised within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Question:
These noble ones follow the sequence exactly as described above.
Is it not the case that such a person fully accomplishes all the paths previously attained?
The answer is: Yes.
One who attains the fruit abandons the previous path; this principle should be understood.
If this person has entered the path, it should be known that they proceed with superior progress; having attained this fruit, they abandon the previous path.
Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause that fruit to revert to a lower stage.
If one were to lose their faculties or advance them, they would likewise abandon the path; however, these cases are not mentioned here.
Upon attaining the fruit of srotāpanna, one abandons the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Upon attaining the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, one either abandons the path of seeing, or abandons the superior path of the srotāpanna fruit.
Upon attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*, one either abandons the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or abandons the superior path of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Upon attaining the fruit of *arhat*, one abandons the fruit of *anāgāmin* and abandons the superior path of the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Regarding the distinction of those who advance their faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*), they both relinquish the path of excellence that constitutes the fruit and attain the fruit.
Those included among those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*)—whether in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—likewise relinquish the fruit and attain the fruit.
If one regresses, one abandons the superior and acquires the inferior. Question:
Just as one who has attained a fruit abandons the path of approach (*pratipannaka-mārga*), does he also abandon the abandonment [of defilements]?
Answer: Abandoning the path is not severance.
That which has already been exhausted constitutes liberation; one attains reliance upon a single fruit.
The ninth [category] is not defiled; one should know that it is abandoned through severance.

Regarding "having exhausted [them], one attains liberation based on a single fruit": the afflictions previously severed are attained through a single acquisition of liberation (vimukti-prāpti), which is subsumed under the attainment of the fruit; therefore, they are not relinquished once severed.
Regarding all paths of liberation within the path toward the Way, one attains such liberation.
Question: The severing of afflictions is as previously explained.
How is that which is non-defiled abandoned?
The answer is:

it should be understood that the non-defiled is abandoned by the ninth [moment]; since it has already been stated that the nine kinds of afflictions are abandoned by the nine kinds of paths, that which is non-defiled is definitely abandoned all at once at the time of the ninth path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), not gradually.
"Non-defiled" refers to wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) states and non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) formations; defiled matter (*rūpa*) is likewise necessarily severed last.
Question: For what reason are the nine types of afflictions severed [first], and not the wholesome and other categories?
Answer: Because it is contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is contrary to the afflictions, but it is not contrary to the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Because they loathe the afflictions (*kleśa*), they also abandon the wholesome; this is because both are bound by the same fetter.
Question: You have already explained the faculties of the Arhat’s progress toward excellence; how does the Arhat attain immovability (*akopya*)?
The answer is:
If there is a name that corresponds [to reality], one can attain immovability;
such a person also possesses faith and liberation, and their nature likewise increases the Path.

If there are those who possess names similar to that of one capable of attaining immovability, it does not mean that all arhats can attain immovability; rather, if their qualities are similar to his, they may attain it, meaning they will certainly advance further.

The statement that "this person, being one liberated by faith, also increases the nature of those who are destined for advancement (prativedhanādharman) so as to attain the state of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)" is incomplete.
If one liberated by faith is destined for advancement, they will necessarily attain the state of one who has attained vision, and not otherwise.
Regarding "increasing the path," this refers to the meaning of the increase of the faculties (*indriya*).
Question: The sequential realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) has already been explained, but its cause has not yet been stated; that cause should now be explained.
Answer: Through the distinction between merit and evil, one successively perceives the Truths;
by the power of the unimpeded path, one attains the conditioned and unconditioned fruits.

Regarding the sequential observation of the distinctions between merit and evil within the Two Truths: herein, there is the distinction between the faults of the Two Truths and the distinction between the merits of the Two Truths. It is not that one who observes faults sees merits, nor is it that one who observes merits sees faults.
Why is this? Because there are distinctions among the conditions for practice.

It is not that one does not attain the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths by seeing them as they truly are; rather, it is not possible for a single cognition to simultaneously contemplate the distinctions between the merits and faults of the truths.
For this reason, one perceives the truths in successive order.
Question: One attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya through the perception of the truths; what are they?
Is this conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The answer is:

By the power of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains both conditioned and unconditioned fruits; if it is the unconditioned fruit consisting in the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), it is unconditioned; if it is the fruit consisting in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is conditioned.
Both of these two types are attained through the power of the path of non-obstruction; therefore, both are described as fruits of the śramaṇa.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Volume Three; *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Volume Four.
The Commentary on the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* by the Venerable Upaśānta, translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Gao Qi period, in six fascicles.
Section Six: Chapter on Wisdom (*Jñānavarga*). This sixth chapter, translated separately, now intends to analyze the wisdom pertaining to the portion of *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? Because wisdom is able to sever all afflictions.
Since one wishes to explain wisdom extensively, this is stated first.
If the nature of wisdom can discern, observing all that exists, both existence and non-existence, and nirvāṇa—I shall now explain their characteristics.
That which is called "existence and non-existence" is nirvāṇa; therefore, the wise observe both existence and non-existence.
"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), meaning the truths of suffering and its origin.
"Non-existence of existence" (*vibhava*) refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Because it encompasses all existence and non-existence, it is called "existence and non-existence"; therein, there is no sense of existence whatsoever.
This explains that there is an antidote, namely cessation; therefore, cessation is not non-existent.
A non-entity cannot have an antidote, as is the case with the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), wherein the mind and mental factors do not function.
The teaching that cessation is a real entity is for the purpose of providing an antidote; thus, nirvāṇa exists as an antidote to all that has its opposite.
This is like the case where, upon removing a disease, one attains health; its characteristic is termed "quiescence."

Regarding such states as quiescence and cessation, the wise observe that the wisdom which takes them as its object does not arise without an objective domain; therefore, when wisdom observes this, it is itself the Path.
Question: What is that? Answer:
The three knowledges taught by the Buddha are the supreme and foremost awakening:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
These three knowledges encompass all forms of knowledge.

Regarding dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna): if a knowledge has the desire realm as its object, or the cessation of the desire realm as its counteractive, or the outflow-free (anāsrava) as its object, and it first apprehends the determination of phenomena, it is therefore called dharma-knowledge.

Conformable knowledge (*anuloma-jñāna*) refers to that knowledge which has the form and formless realms as its object, the cessation of the form and formless realms as its counteragent, or the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object; because it follows in immediate succession after the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it is called conformable knowledge.

Regarding "worldly wisdom" (*saṃvṛtijñāna*): if there is outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravajñāna*) that frequently engages with conventional designations—such as "man," "woman," and so forth—it is called worldly wisdom; such categories are termed "worldly wisdom."
Regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, two types of knowledge arise accordingly;
these four kinds of knowledge the Muni taught according to their names.
As for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), they proceed in accordance with the Noble Truths.
The World-Honored One speaks according to names; because it is the objective sphere of the Truth of Suffering, he speaks of "knowledge of suffering.

Likewise, because they are the objective spheres of the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, they are called "knowledge of origination," "knowledge of cessation," and "knowledge of the path."

Regarding the distinction between the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two knowledges—of suffering (*duḥkha*) and of origination (*samudaya*): when the mode of activity is directed toward suffering, it is termed the knowledge of suffering; when the mode of activity is directed toward origination, it is termed the knowledge of origination.

As for their objects (*ālambana*), there is no distinction, as both equally take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their object. Therefore, the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) differ in both their modes of activity and their objects.

If wisdom observes the minds of others, it is said to arise from three [knowledges]; the two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising should be known to reside in four gates. Regarding the statement that "if wisdom observes the minds of others, it is said to arise from three":

among the three knowledges, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is, when contaminated (*sāsrava*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
