In the second part of the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* of the sixth fascicle, having already explained the intrinsic nature of the qualities (*guṇa*) and their being with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), their accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*) shall now be explained.
One should know that those who have not yet abandoned desire accomplish the meditative attainments associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*);
those who have abandoned lower levels but not yet reached higher ones accomplish the pure (*śuddha*) meditative attainments.

Regarding the statement "one should know that those who have not yet abandoned desire accomplish the meditative attainments associated with relish": if a person has not yet abandoned desire for a particular level, they accomplish the meditative attainments associated with relish belonging to that level.

Regarding "one who has departed from the lower but not yet reached the upper achieves the pure [attainments]": this refers to one who has departed from the desires of the desire realm but has not yet given rise to the second dhyāna and so forth within the Brahma-world; whether they have departed from desire or have not departed from desire, they achieve the pure first dhyāna as well as other virtuous qualities belonging to that stage.
One should know that abiding in the higher [stages], one accomplishes the lower untainted [states];
this is the merit produced through skillful means, and one should know it is not apart from the abandonment of desire.

Regarding "one should know that abiding in the higher [stages], one accomplishes the lower untainted [states]": when a noble person is born in the Brahma-world, they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna as well as other untainted samādhis, supernormal powers, knowledge, and all such merits.

In those stages, the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) merits constitute the bondage of the place of birth, while the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) constitutes the severance of that bondage; therefore, one abandons the outflow-tainted by departing from the place of birth, not the outflow-free.
This applies to all stages according to their respective meanings.

One should know that the production of merit through skillful means does not belong to those who have not yet abandoned desire; for it has already been stated that the accomplishment of various merits belongs to those who have abandoned the desires of the lower stages. One should know that this refers to the attainment of accomplishment, though it is not currently manifest.
Regarding the application of skillful means (*upāya*) being present before one, that is not the abandonment of desire.

As for the attainment through skillful means—such as the divine eye and ear—it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, it is not included within the untainted (*anāsrava*), the pure (*śuddha*), or that associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*). Consequently, when one attains those three types of dhyāna, one does not attain the cessation [of perception and feeling], because the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is itself the application of skillful means.
He attains twenty-three kinds of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) present before him:
eight associated with the flavorful (*sāsvāda*), eight pure (*śuddha*), and seven untainted (*anāsrava*). Question:
Regarding how many kinds of causes there are for each of those,
the answer is:
what is called untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) has seven kinds of causes for each.
Regarding the meditative absorptions associated with the purity of taste (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta-dhyāna*), one should know that they have one cause.

As for what are called the seven types of causes for each instance of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*): each instance of the untainted has seven types [of causes]. Among these, within the untainted, those that are "causes by way of their own class" (*sabhāga-hetu*) and "causes by way of their own level" (*svabhūmi-hetu*) are also "associated causes" (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and "co-arising causes" (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Regarding the statement that "one should know that the dhyāna associated with relish has one cause": this refers to the first dhyāna associated with relish.

The first dhyāna associated with relish has as its cause only itself and nothing else, because the causes of the first dhyāna are not similar [to those of other levels]; nor is it the cause of the defiled states of other stages, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are contradictory.
It is contrary to the aspect of defiled [states], yet it is not its own-part (sabhāga).
Thus, the pure first dhyāna is the cause of the pure first dhyāna; it is neither defiled nor untainted (anāsrava).
Why is this? Because they are dissimilar.
They are not the pure causes of other stages, because they are the retribution of their own stage and are bound to their own stage.
Thus it is for all. It is asked:
How many kinds arise in each successive stage?
The answer is:

The untainted dhyānas and formless attainments—whether practiced in reverse order, forward order, or by skipping stages—produce six types of births in sequence; one should know that this continues up to ten.

From the untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna, six types arise in succession: the pure (śuddha) and untainted states of its own level; likewise for the second and third dhyānas; such is the meditative attainment of transcendence (vyutkrāntakasamāpatti).
From the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), seven states arise in succession:
two from its own level, four from lower levels, and one from a higher level.
From the untainted second dhyāna, eight states arise in succession:
From its own level, two; from the level of the first dhyāna, two; and from the higher levels, four.
From the uncontaminated (anāsrava) sphere of infinite consciousness, nine arise in succession:
two from its own level, four from the lower levels, and three from the higher levels.
The remaining untainted [attainments] arise in succession from ten:
two from their own level, four from the lower levels, and four from the higher levels.
Or, from six up to eleven—this refers to the arising in succession of the pure [attainments].
From two up to ten, one should know that these are said to be associated with the "taste" (*āsvādana*).

As for the statement "or six up to eleven, which arise in succession from the pure": when the pure [attainment] arises in succession from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), six [types of mind] arise:

those associated with the taste of its own level, the four pure [minds] of the lower levels, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) [mind]; they are not associated with the taste because of the absence of desire.
From the pure first dhyāna, seven [minds] arise in succession:
three from its own level and four from higher levels—namely, the pure and the untainted [minds].
From the pure sphere of nothingness, eight [minds] arise in succession:
Three from its own level, one from a higher level, and four from lower levels.
Nine arise in succession from the pure second dhyāna; ten arise in succession from the sphere of infinite consciousness; and eleven from the remaining [levels].
All such cases should be understood as referring to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), not the time of death.

Therefore, within that state, the flavors associated with the higher and lower stages are not included; rather, the innate pure (*upapatti-lābhika-śuddha*) states arise in succession, accompanied by the flavors of the higher and lower stages.
It should be understood that from two up to ten, those described as "having relish" (sāsvāda) arise in succession from the first dhyāna associated with relish; specifically, two states arise:
that which is associated with relish belonging to its own level and the pure (śuddhaka), because these two are not mutually contradictory.
There are ten successive states arising from the flavor-associated [attainment] of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra):

three flavors of meditative attainment (samāpatti), two of its own level, and the pure (śuddha) of the lower levels; because it is afflicted by the defilements of its own level, one relies on the purity of the sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) to protect oneself.

In this way, all [attainments] of a lower stage are purified by a lower stage; furthermore, at the time of death, one may fall from a higher stage to a lower stage—all of these are associated with relish (*āsvādana*).
Question: Previously, you spoke of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
The afflictions shall now be explained.
The answer is:

regarding the pure successive attainments (*śuddhānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the afflictions are described as being associated with relish (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) and as afflictions pertaining to rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*).
Why is this? Because afflictions arise through the power of [mental] instability, not through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, it is said here that the purification of all afflictions necessarily depends on the power of meditative concentration; for this reason, it is said that afflictions coexist with meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Question: Among those, how many kinds of objects does each one take as its condition? Answer:
Pure and untainted dhyānas operate across all stages; they take as their objects the tainted phenomena of their own stage and those associated with relishing (*āsvādanasamprayukta*).
Regarding "pure and untainted dhyānas operate across all stages": pure and untainted dhyānas take all stages and all things as their objects.

Regarding the objects of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) within their own stage: these consist of the states associated with relishing and the pure (*śuddhaka*) states of that same stage; they do not include the untainted (*anāsrava*). Why is this?
It does not have the untainted as its object;
craving for existence also does not take other stages as its object.
It does not function in the formless realm, but rather toward tainted phenomena in the lower realms.
If the root is wholesome, it is defiled like the dhyānas of taste.

As for "the formless [attainments] do not operate upon the outflowing (sāsrava) matters of the lower [stages]," this means that the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) do not take the outflowing dharmas of the lower stages as their object.

Why is this? Because the lower stages are not quiescent. Furthermore, they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the lower stages as objects, just as in the case of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Question: Do all contaminated states not take lower levels as their object? Answer: No.
Not so; if it is fundamental, it is wholesome.
If it is fundamental, pure, or untainted formless [attainment], it takes its own level and higher levels as objects, but does not take lower levels as objects.
If future-dhyāna takes a lower stage as its object, it feels revulsion toward the coarse perceptions of that lower stage.
Regarding defiled [dhyāna] being like dhyāna associated with relishing: as it was explained for dhyāna associated with relishing, so it is for the defiled formless attainments.
If there are remaining immeasurable and other virtues in the form realm, they have the desire realm as their object; this is what the World-Honored One has taught.
As for the virtues of the form realm—namely, the four immeasurables, the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth—they take the desire realm as their objective support.
For what reason are "immeasurable" and so forth taught apart from the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
Those five supernormal powers take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their objects. Question:
As previously stated regarding the cultivation of wisdom within perfumed dhyāna, how is it perfumed?
The answer is:
"If one can perfume the various dhyānas, this relies upon the fourth dhyāna."
Because craving for the third dhyāna has been exhausted, the Śuddhāvāsa heavens consist solely of the Bṛhatphala.
If one is able to perfuse the various dhyānas by relying on the fourth dhyāna, it is only through the attainment of the fourth dhyāna that one can perfuse the dhyānas, and not otherwise.

That person repeatedly enters the untainted (anāsrava) four dhyānas and emerges from them to repeatedly enter the tainted (sāsrava) dhyānas; then returning again to the untainted and again to the tainted, they gradually abbreviate the process until abiding for only two kṣaṇas.
By such means, whether it be a single untainted mind or a single tainted mind—at that time, one thought-moment is tainted and one thought-moment is untainted.
When two moments consist of one tainted and one untainted, this is called "accomplishment."
Question: Where is this fruit attained? Answer:
Among the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
Why is this? Because craving for the three lower stages has been exhausted; thus, the Śuddhāvāsas consist solely of the Bṛhatphala [heaven].
If one attains the fourth dhyāna by becoming detached from the craving of the three lower stages, one is therefore a person who has attained the fourth dhyāna.

Within the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) and the Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala), ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) collectively cultivate the perfumed dhyāna (vāsita-dhyāna). Regarding those who do not share with ordinary beings, there are five types: inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and supreme.
These five types—Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha—are the heavens; therefore, one attains the fruit therein.
Question: As previously stated, what are these seven kinds of knowledge resulting from vows? Answer:
Unattached and immovable in the Dharma, he attains all meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
By the power of that samādhi-knowledge, he is able to give rise to the "summit" of the fourth dhyāna.
Because his mental continuum is thus, afflictions cannot oppress or disturb him.
Because the mental continuum arises through the power of all correct aspirations, one attains three virtues:
namely, the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), and the unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding that knowledge resulting from aspiration: if one wishes to know the past, future, present, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), at that time one abides in the limit of the knowledge resulting from aspiration and, through the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the fourth dhyāna, is able to know them.

"Non-contention" (araṇā) means not desiring to give rise to the contention of afflictions within the mental continuums of others; such a person does not cause the contention of afflictions to arise in the mental continuums of others.
"Unimpededness" (araṇā) is as previously explained.
Question: By which stage (bhūmi) is the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) subsumed? Answer:
The knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) exists in the third dhyāna; the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) exists within the fifth dhyāna;
the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) exist in the second dhyāna; and two of the analytical knowledges rely upon all nine stages.
Regarding "the knowledge resulting from resolve exists in the third [dhyāna]," this refers to the fourth dhyāna, the first dhyāna, and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It is definitely attained within the fourth dhyāna. In the desire realm, only among humans can one give rise to a mind associated with the Brahma-world of the desire realm; since the mind that initiates verbal expression exists there, it is said to belong to three stages.
Regarding the five stages of the absence of conflict (*araṇā*): they consist of the four fundamental dhyānas and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is definitely attained within the four dhyānas; it can be produced among human beings and not in other places.

Regarding the analytical knowledge of dharma and language (*dharmapada-pratisaṃvid*) on the second stage: as for the analytical knowledge of dharma (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), it pertains to five stages: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), which consist of the four fundamental dhyānas and the desire realm itself.
These are merely objects of names; since speech proceeds from names, it is through them that the path of language arises.
The eloquence of speech is said to exist in places where there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), namely, in the desire realm and the Brahma-world. Why is this?
Because it has speech as its object-condition.

Second, regarding the classification by the nine stages (*bhūmi*): the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratibhāna*) are comprised within the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the fundamental first dhyāna.
Question: How does one attain this right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)? Answer:
Through detachment and through rebirth, one attains pure dhyāna;
through defilement, retrogression, and rebirth, [one attains the defiled]; the untainted is attained only through detachment.
Regarding "through detachment and through rebirth, one attains pure dhyāna": pure first dhyāna is attained at two times.
When one attains detachment from desire, or when passing away from a higher stage and being reborn in the Brahma-world, one acquires the abandonment of that stage; all such cases are like this.

Regarding the defiled [attainments] acquired through falling back or through birth: in the case of the dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), one falls back from a higher stage and acquires a lower one; or, within the second dhyāna, one falls back due to the fetters of the desire realm or the fetters of the Brahma-world—at that time, one acquires [the defiled attainment].

Regarding the attainment of the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) through birth: when one dies in a higher plane and is born into the desire realm or the Brahma-world, at that time one attains the first dhyāna associated with relishing; all such cases are like this.
Regarding "the untainted [attainments] belong only to those free from desire": the untainted dhyānas are obtained through the abandonment of desire.

This means that when a noble one abandons the desires of the desire realm, they obtain the untainted first dhyāna; because it was not previously obtained, it is now obtained, and so it is for all [subsequent stages].
Question: Among these merits, which one is able to eliminate the afflictions? Answer:
The untainted removes the afflictions; for those in the intermediate state of meditative attainment, all states between concentrations are associated with the faculty of equanimity.
"The untainted removes the afflictions" means that the untainted dhyānas and formless attainments remove the afflictions, whereas the mundane ones do not.
Question: Why does the conventional [wisdom] not sever the afflictions? Answer:
Because they share the same bondage:
in conventional reality, the afflictions are bound together as one; therefore, the afflictions of their own level cannot sever themselves.
It is like a person who has been tied with a back-knot and cannot untie it himself, unless that which serves as the antidote or the means of severance arises.
Question: Is it the case that all worldly [paths] cannot sever the afflictions? Answer:
There is a mundane [path] capable of severing the afflictions. Question: What is it?
The answer is:

"In the midst of meditative attainment" refers to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-dhyāna*), wherein one has not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas, but through the application of skillful means, one becomes detached from the desires of the lower realm.
In that first dhyāna, the future states are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), whereas the remaining future states are exclusively with-outflows.
Since these serve as the basis for the fundamental dhyānas and formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), it is therefore said that the mundane [path] does not sever the afflictions (kleśa).
Question: Where is this preliminary dhyāna located? Answer:
In all intermediate states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Within all states of right attainment (*samyaksamāpatti*), one is associated with the faculty of equanimity; because that which is sought has not yet been attained, joy (*prīti*) does not arise.

Question: Although the supernormal power of the domain of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) and the supernormal power of realization through knowledge (jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā) have been explained, it has not yet been stated how many kinds of transformative minds (nirmāṇacitta) there are; this shall now be explained. Answer:
Fourteen are the fruits of the desire realm and the first dhyāna:

the fruit of the first dhyāna belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; the fruit of the second dhyāna belonging to the desire realm; the fruit of the second dhyāna belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; and the fruit of the second dhyāna belonging to the level of the second dhyāna. This continues in the same manner up to the fourth dhyāna.
Question: Who accomplishes that? Answer:
The transformation-mind of a lower stage accomplishes the fruit of its own seeds;
corresponding to that consciousness, it is accomplished in those higher stages.

Regarding "the transformation-mind of a lower stage accomplishes the fruit of its own seeds": if a person accomplishes dhyāna, that person accomplishes the fruit of that [dhyāna], which is the transformation-mind of the lower stage.

Just as when one attains the first dhyāna, the fruit of the first dhyāna is accomplished within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) which is the ground of that first dhyāna; so it should be understood in all such cases.

Question: You previously stated that the second dhyāna and those above lack the five bodies of consciousness (pañca-vijñānakāya). If one is born in those higher stages and wishes to see or hear, how does one see or hear?
Answer: The consciousness of the Brahma-world manifests before one. Question:
Why is this consciousness absent in the higher stages?
The answer is:
because they lack vitarka and vicāra.
Question: For how long is that accomplished? Answer:

In accordance with whichever consciousness is associated with them, those [faculties] of the higher stages are accomplished; that is to say, they are accomplished at the time when whichever consciousness is associated [with them]—whether it be visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, or tactile consciousness—is present at that moment. They are accomplished at that very time.
The cessation of this consciousness is called "equanimity" (upekṣā).
Why? Because it is dependent upon the sense faculties (indriya).
Chapter Eight: The Sūtra Chapter. Regarding the most profound and subtle meanings spoken from the mouth of the Omniscient One, I shall now explain what remains.
The mouth of the Omniscient One speaks of meanings that are profound and subtle;
I shall now explain a small portion of them—listen attentively to this sutra.
It is asked:
As the Buddha taught regarding the three realms, what are they?
The answer is:
there are ten abodes in the desire realm, and seventeen are said to be in the form realm.
The formless realm has four [levels], which definitely exist only there.
As for the ten abodes of the desire realm, they refer to the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the various classes of the six heavens of the desire realm.
These ten abodes should be understood as describing the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); for in these places, the conceptualization of desire (*kāmasaṃjñā*) arises in sentient beings.
Since all those things associated with craving and desire are fully present here, it is therefore called the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that there are seventeen levels in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha—these seventeen abodes are said to constitute the realm of form.

In this abode, the perception of desire does not arise; because those [beings] possess extremely great form that lacks the characteristics of male or female, it is therefore called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the four [levels] of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):

there are four abodes in the Formless Realm—namely, the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
In this dwelling, form does not arise.
Why is this? Because of the abandonment of desire for form.
Furthermore, because there is sequential cessation, if form were to arise within the formless, there would be no sequential cessation; yet sequential cessation does exist.
If it did not exist, there would be the fault of desire arising from within form. Therefore, form does not arise within the formless, and for this reason it is called "formless."

Question: As the Buddha has taught the three realms of existence— existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—
what does this mean?
Answer: It is determined that they exist only there.
That which was previously described as the "elements" (dhātu) is precisely what exists here.
Question: As the Blessed One has spoken of the seven stations of consciousness, what are they? Answer:
The happy destinies (*sugati*) consist of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the three levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the three levels of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
one should know these to be the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Within the happy destinies of the desire realm, these are reckoned as humans and devas.

The first three stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the first three stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); these seven stages are said to be the abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Question:
For what reason are the three evil destinies, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) not called abodes of consciousness?
The answer is:

If a stage (*bhūmi*) is subject to abandonment through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), yet gives rise to consciousness that is not abandoned, it is called a station of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

Within the three evil destinies, there is no matter that is not abandoned; likewise, among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) and the Śuddhāvāsa deities in the fourth dhyāna, there is no matter abandoned through seeing. Therefore, the fourth dhyāna is not included [among the stations of consciousness].
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*); if consciousness dwells in pleasure there, it is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
In the three evil realms, consciousness does not dwell in pleasure. Why is this?
Because it is oppressed by suffering, and because the Śuddhāvāsa deities are oriented toward nirvāṇa, consciousness does not dwell there with pleasure.
Furthermore, the beings in the state of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) are likewise entirely without mind; therefore, this [state] is not included within the fourth dhyāna.
The activity in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not swift; therefore, it is also not included. There are three kinds of sentient beings:
those who delight in objects, those who delight in pleasure, and those who delight in the perception of pleasure.

Among them, "those who delight in objects" refers to humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); "those who delight in pleasure" refers to the third dhyāna stage; and "those who delight in the perception of pleasure" refers to the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). For this reason, these are described as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Question: What are the nine abodes of sentient beings? Answer:
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the Non-percipient [beings]—these are said to be the abodes of sentient beings.
The four kinds of contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) should be known as the stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

Regarding "the Peak of Existence and the Non-percipient [beings] are said to be the abodes of sentient beings": previously, seven stations of consciousness were taught; together with the Heaven of Non-perception and the Peak of Existence, these are here stated to be the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Question: For what reason are the evil realms and the non-percipient beings excluded from being called "abodes of sentient beings" within the fourth dhyāna? Answer:
Wherever one wishes to dwell and has no desire to depart, that place is called a "dwelling of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*).
In the evil realms, these two conditions do not exist; and although those in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven wish to dwell there, they also wish to depart.
Question: As the Buddha taught the four stations of consciousness (*catur-vijñāna-sthiti*), what are they? Answer:
The four kinds of contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) should be known as the abodes of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Contaminated form, feeling, perception, and formations—these are called aggregates and are described as the abodes of consciousness.
Because consciousness arises together with grasping (*upādāna*), dwells, clings, and is nourished therein, they are therefore called the abodes of consciousness.

Therefore, the untainted (*anāsrava*) is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), because it destroys existence (*bhava*); nor is it a place where consciousness dwells in conjunction with grasping (*upādāna*).
Question: Why is consciousness itself not a station of consciousness?
Answer: That reason is unestablished.
It is like the royal road; the king is not the road itself.

The co-emergent consciousness (*sahaja-vijñāna*) that belongs to the category of non-abiding is called the "abode" (*sthāna*); the triad of conditions is called the "abode," but this consciousness is not like that.
Question: Is there no other consciousness present as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?

Answer: Because it does not arise from its own combination, that [self] is also not established; furthermore, it is both included among the category of sentient beings and not included among the category of sentient beings. Question:
How is it that external objects serve as the basis for the abiding of consciousness?
The answer is:

there is no fault because they arise together in combination and abide by way of being dependent conditions in great number; furthermore, those [objects] serve as conditions for the abiding of that [consciousness] within its own respective sphere (*dhātu*), not in another sphere.
Question: As the Blessed One has taught the twelve links of dependent origination, what are their characteristics? Answer:
The various afflictions and karmas, along with their bases, arise in succession;
know that these are the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), which constitute the entire birth of sentient beings.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are the afflictions; volitional formations and becoming are karma; the remaining links are the bases.
Thus, these factors of affliction, karma, and the objective basis arise sequentially within various births; therefore, they are called the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Among them, the afflictions depend upon the objective basis; the afflictions perform the function of karma, and karma performs the function of the objective basis.

Thus it is. Those constituent factors are established as follows: namely, the birth of sentient beings in the past, the future, and the intermediate state; one should know that there are eight [factors] therein.
The establishment of those factors refers to the birth of sentient beings; these distinct factors are explained as the twelve links.
Question: What are they?
The answer is:
Regarding the past and the future, one should know that there are eight in the intermediate [period].
Among these, "ignorance" refers to the afflictions of the past.
"Conduct" refers to past karma.
"Consciousness" refers to the continuous mind and its attendants.

"Name-and-form" refers to that which has already received birth and is bound in a continuous succession without ceasing, yet before the four types of material sense-faculties have arisen and the six sense-bases are incomplete; this is called name-and-form.

Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): when the four types of material sense organs have already arisen but are not yet able to serve as the basis for contact, this stage is called the six sense bases.

Regarding contact (*sparśa*): when these sense organs are already able to serve as the basis for contact but are not yet able to distinguish between pleasure and pain, nor able to distinguish between gain and loss, this stage is called contact.

Feeling (vedanā) is that which can distinguish the causes of suffering and pleasure, gain and loss; it is able to know the distinctions among nutriments and to discern craving so as not to give rise to sensual desire—this stage is called feeling.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the state of longing for and seeking after the objects of desire; when one is unable to obtain them and engages in conceptual discrimination, this is called craving.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is the act of seizing and conceptual discrimination.

"Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to the rapid pursuit and inclination toward those objective spheres, which extensively produces the various realms of existence for future birth; at that time, it is called "becoming.
"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to the sequential continuity and the binding of links following death; at that time, it is called "birth."
Regarding "old age and death": the subsequent [stages] of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, are called old age and death.
Question: The World-Honored One spoke of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*); what does this refer to?
The answer is:
What are called the four great elements, as well as all contaminated consciousnesses, are seen within form; these realms are said to be the basis of arising.

Regarding the statement that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and all contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) are also seen as being within form: this refers to the four great elements, the five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*), the contaminated mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*), and the space reckoned as that which is apprehended by the apertures of the eyes; these are called the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*).
Question: For what reason are six elements specifically mentioned among the eighteen elements? Answer:

This realm is said to be the basis for the conception of a "person. That which is the basis for the arising of those phenomena is here designated by the term "person. It is established upon the earth element; it is moistened and saturated by the water element; it is ripened and its foul odors removed by the fire element; it is moved by the wind element; and within the space of the internal cavities, food and drink enter and exit. Through the power of the corresponding consciousness, it is established and thus receives the name "conception of a person."
Therefore, this is called the "perception of elements" (dhātu-saṃjñā). Why?
Because it is the nature of arising.
As the Blessed One said:
"By reason of the six elements and by way of conditions, one enters the mother’s womb.
Such is the scriptural passage (*sūtra-pada*).
That great [element] also arises; therefore, it is called "great arising.

Just as with the "great beings" (mahāsattva) and "great birth" (mahotpāda), herein the earth has the characteristic of solidity, water the characteristic of moisture, fire the characteristic of heat, wind the characteristic of lightness and motion, and the perception of the limits of form is called the space element (ākāśadhātu).
Form (rūpa) is that which differs from volition (cetanā); consciousness (vijñāna) is characterized by cognizing.
Question: What are the characteristics of the Noble Truths?
The answer is:
Conditioned phenomena that resemble their fruit, being with outflows (*sāsrava*), are called suffering;
those resembling their cause are the origin; and the cessation of all suffering is the truth of cessation.

Regarding the statement that "conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) similar to the fruit, which are with outflows (sāsrava), are called suffering": all conditioned phenomena with outflows arise from causes and possess the characteristic of oppression;

therefore, they are called suffering. Regarding "those similar to the cause are the origin (samudaya)": all conditioned phenomena with outflows are similar to other causes; therefore, they are called the origin of suffering.
Just as a single grain of rice is called both fruit and cause when viewed in relation to what precedes and follows it, so too,

conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called both suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) because they are observed in relation to what has already arisen and what is yet to arise.
Regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), the complete exhaustion and extinction of all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) is called the truth of cessation.
As for uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*), these are called the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Because of these two designations, they are perceived in sequence from the coarse [to the subtle].
If all untainted conditioned phenomena are said to be the Truth of the Path, then all untainted phenomena are called the Truth of the Path because they constitute the cessation of all suffering.
Question: For what reason are they called "truths" (satya)? Answer:

Because of these two kinds of names and these two kinds of objects, they are called truths (*satya*): namely, the non-falsity of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the realization of the non-perverted mind that perceives their arising.
Question:
Why are space and analytical cessation not subsumed under the [Noble] Truths?
The answer is:
because they are neither cause nor effect.
Because this observation is for the sake of the exhaustion of suffering, it is an observation of the Noble Truths;
it does not concern that which is not suffering, nor the cause of suffering, nor the means for the departure from suffering, but observes solely with the desire to exhaust suffering.
It is, for example, like the cause of a disease, the medicine for the disease, and the recovery from the disease—just as one observes a disease.
Question: What is the meaning of the Noble Truths?
The answer is:
Because the Noble Ones have realized them as they truly are and then revealed them to others, they are called "Noble Truths.

Among these, the characteristic of oppression is suffering (*duḥkha*), the characteristic of origination is accumulation (*samudaya*), the characteristic of tranquility is cessation (*nirodha*), and the characteristic of renunciation is the path (*mārga*).
Question: Since one perceives that the effect exists because of the cause, why does the Buddha first speak of the effect and later speak of the cause? Answer:
One perceives them in order from the coarse; thus, one perceives only the [Four Noble Truths] through direct realization (*abhisamaya*). Therefore, the Blessed One previously taught the fruits first:
the practitioner first attains the direct realization of suffering, then its cause, then its cessation, and finally the path.
Why is this? Because one first realizes the fruit and subsequently abandons the cause, as wisdom arises through cultivation.

Once that practitioner has directly realized the intrinsic nature of suffering, at that time, for the sake of abandoning the cause of suffering, decisive knowledge arises, because [suffering] is the cause of affliction.

In this way, that practitioner first perceives the characteristic of cessation; at that time, desiring to realize cessation, he cultivates skillful means and gives rise to definitive knowledge. For this reason, the fruit is explained first.
Thus, because one first perceives the coarse and subsequently perceives the subtle;
because suffering is coarse and its origin is subtle, due to the process of designation, investigation, and faith;
and because cessation is coarse and the path is subtle—for these reasons, cessation is taught first and the path is taught afterwards.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Bhikṣu should explain cessation for them, and explain the path leading to cessation for their sake. And so forth.
Therefore, one first seeks cessation and subsequently cultivates the path.
It is like the road to a city: one first finds the road and only then enters the city.
All people believe in cessation but do not understand the path; thus, for the sake of easy comprehension, it is explained according to the sequence of the coarse.
Question: The World-Honored One has spoken of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; how many factors do they consist of? Answer:
The matters of the noble fruits are six; the most excellent resides in the nine stages, the third resides in the six stages, and two kinds depend on the future stage.
Regarding "the matters of the noble fruits are six," six matters are taught as the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Question: What is the meaning of "fruit of the ascetic life" (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)?
Answer: The Noble Path is called the śramaṇa; because one achieves it through diligence, it is named the fruit of the śramaṇa. Question:
The mundane path is also attained by a man of diligence; does he also attain the fruits of śramaṇaship?
Answer: He perceives the distinctions among the fruits of the noble path.
Question: What is the fruit of this, and by which stage (bhūmi) is it subsumed? Answer:
The most excellent [fruit] resides in nine stages; the fruit of arhatship is comprised within nine stages:
the preliminary stage (anāgāmya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (ārūpyas).
The third [fruit] resides in six stages; the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) is comprised within six stages, excluding the formless attainments.
The two types [of fruits] depend on the future; that is, the fruits of srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin are subsumed within the future. Why is this?
Because they have not yet abandoned desire.
Question: What are the characteristics of the tracks? Answer:
The dharmas of the faith-follower (śraddhānusārin) are characterized by the absence of afflictions and dull faculties;
the dharmas of the dharma-follower (dharmānusārin) are characterized by the absence of afflictions and swift [faculties].

Regarding "the dharmas of the faith-follower are characterized by the absence of afflictions and dull faculties": when the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of a faith-follower are comprised within the weak stage, it should be understood that they are categorized as dull faith-followers.
It should be known that those liberated through faith and those liberated by occasion are also included because they possess dull faculties.

Regarding the characteristics of the rapid attainment of the various dharmas for those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmanusārin*), it should be known that because their own dharmas are subsumed under sharp faculties, the characteristic of rapidity is likewise subsumed therein. It should also be known that the characteristics of the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those not liberated by occasion (*asamayavimukta*) are similarly included.
Why is this? Because their faculties are sharp.
Within that fundamental dhyāna, one should know that this is the penetration of bliss.
Because it is minor and difficult to attain, one should know that the remaining [states] are described as suffering.

Regarding the statement that "within the fundamental dhyānas, one should know this bliss is pervasive": in the four fundamental dhyānas, whether they pertain to those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) or sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*), one should know them to be the path of bliss, because one attains the Way through the equilibrium of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), and because they constitute a pleasant practice.

Because it is minor and difficult to obtain, one should know that when others speak of suffering, they refer to the path subsumed under the untainted stages (*anāsrava-bhūmi*) as "suffering" because it is so slight; for in those states—the future dhyāna and the intermediate dhyāna—the path of cessation is minimal.
Among the formless realms (*ārūpya*), few uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states are observed; they are difficult to attain in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*). Why is this?
Because the mundane [attainments] are obtained from the preparatory stage; by attaining those, it is easy to cultivate dhyāna.

In the intermediate dhyāna, at the stage of the single ground, the cessation of mind and mental factors manifests; that is to say, the abandonment of *vitarka* (applied thought) and the manifestation of *vicāra* (sustained thought) are accomplished, like cutting wood with wood.

In the formless realm, the subtle and difficult-to-accomplish five aggregates undergo successive cessation, and the four aggregates successively manifest. That difficulty is such because it is hard to attain; therefore, it is called "difficult."
The Noble Path is not suffering; by its very nature, it is not associated with the sensation of suffering, for it is established therein as the supreme path.
Because it has the sense of entering the city of Nirvāṇa, it is called the "sense of the track."
Question: What are the invincibles? Answer:
The Buddha and the teachings of the śrāvakas, liberation and other causes, pure and stainless faith, and noble ethical discipline are what is called "certainty.

Regarding "the Buddha and the teachings of the śrāvakas, liberation and other causes, pure and stainless faith": the Buddha is the one possessing the wisdom of perfect awakening in all its aspects; the Buddha-dharmas are the qualities subsumed within those arhats.
It should be understood that within that context, if there is untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*), it is called "unshakable confidence in the Buddha.

As for the śrāvaka who has attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the instruction of another, it should be understood that among those [who have attained] the śrāvaka-dharma of training and beyond-training (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*), if there is untainted faith, that is "unshakable confidence in the Saṃgha."

Whether it be faith in nirvāṇa or faith in the untainted (*anāsrava*), which extends to other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) such as the truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and origination (*samudayasatya*); such untainted faith in the qualities of a bodhisattva, the states of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha—this indestructible faith in all dharmas is pure right faith regarding suffering and origination, and is the faith of aspiration regarding cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
The untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) arise simultaneously with the Noble Path as the fourth unshakable confidence (*avekṣaṇīya*).
Why is it called "unshakable"?
Because knowing [the truth] and being decisively purified, this is called unshakable confidence (*akopya-prasāda*).
Question: What is it that, when known, is not destroyed? Answer:
Regarding the Four Noble Truths,
it is asked:
Why is there untainted, indestructible faith?
Answer: Because it is definitive.
That untainted faith and precepts co-arising with true knowledge are definitive; as for tainted faith, they are able to obstruct, disparage, and refute it.

Observance of precepts, breaking of precepts, reviling, deception, and hindering the outflows—these, and others that do not arise, can act as hindrances and deceptions; therefore, it is determined that there are distinctions within the indestructible faith in the outflow-free state.
Question: What are the characteristics of the cultivation of meditative concentration? Answer:
If the first dhyāna is wholesome, one should know it is the happiness of the present life;
that is, attaining knowledge of birth and death—this is called "knowledge and vision.

Regarding the statement, "If the first dhyāna is wholesome, one should know it is the happiness of the present life": the pure and untainted first dhyāna is dwelling in the happiness of the present life; this is called attaining the happiness of the present life through the cultivation of concentration.

That which is called "attaining the knowledge of birth and death" refers to one who possesses knowledge and vision; this knowledge of birth and death is said to be the supernormal power attained through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One should understand that wisdom (*prajñā*) performs the discernment [of phenomena]. Through skillful means (*upāya*), one generates merit;
the diamond-like fourth dhyāna is what is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Regarding the statement, "One should know that the wisdom of discernment arises from skillful means and produces merit": all merit produced through skillful means—including the merit of the precepts with manifest instruction (*vijñapti-śīla*), as well as the merit of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*) within the desire realm, and whatever exists throughout the three realms, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)—all of these are called the wisdom of discernment acquired through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā-labdha-vicaya-prajñā*).

Regarding the statement that the diamond-like fourth dhyāna is called "the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*): the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is associated with its attendant factors as the final mind of a learner (*śaikṣa*). Because the outflows are exhausted within the stage of the fourth dhyāna, this is described as the cultivation of concentration.

This is what the Blessed One himself declared regarding his own qualities: that while a bodhisattva was in the first dhyāna absorption within the shadow of a Jambu tree, he dwelt in the joy of seeing the Dharma.
There are eleven types of afflictions; the vision of the pure divine eye and wisdom is as described in the *Pukkusa Sutta*.

That sutra states that one realizes the distinctions of wisdom, such as knowing the arising of feeling, and based on the fourth dhyāna, realizes the exhaustion of outflows through unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of the bases of psychic power?
The answer is:
The wholesome conditioned dharmas arise from skillful means;
the Buddha calls them the bases of psychic power, and these are also called right exertion.

Regarding what the Buddha called the "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), which arise through skillful means (*upāya*) regarding all conditioned wholesome phenomena: because those phenomena arising from such skillful means are said to be the instruments for all that is willed, they are called the bases of psychic power.
The various merits arise through mastery over one's own mind; the accomplishment of these is called the *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power).
"Pāda" (foot), "aṅga" (limb), "sambhāra" (equipment), and "hetu" (cause) are synonymous.
What is meant by samādhi? It refers to the fourfold distinctions of predominance (*adhipati*).
For example, when samādhi arises with desire as its predominant factor, it is called "desire-samādhi" (*chanda-samādhi*).
When such diligence gives rise to mental predominance, it is called the "discriminative samādhi.

Because one first initiates desire, desire is predominant; once desire has arisen, one seeks to attain what is desired through that desire, and thus diligence and concentration become predominant. Once diligence has been initiated, the mind that does not abandon diligence but follows and inclines toward it is called "mental concentration" (citta-samādhi).

When the principle of this desire, diligence, and mind manifests before one, it reaches ultimate fulfillment within the body as the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); therefore, it is called the samādhi of wisdom (*prajñā-samādhi*).
If one does not discriminate against anything else, this single-mindedness accomplishes everything, for it arises within all states of mind.
Because those [qualities] increase through the differentiation of skillful means (*upāya*), other virtues are taught.
Those are also said to be "rightly incinerated" (*samyag-dagdha*); these aforementioned virtues are likewise said to be "rightly incinerated."
Because it is able to burn away the grass of afflictions through reasoning, it is called "right burning" (*samyag-dāha*).

Alternatively, because it is able to sever the afflictions, it is called "right abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*); and because one enters into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), it is called "right victory" (*samyag-vijaya*).
The right effort (*vīrya-saṃskāra*) is that which abandons faults and evils, gives rise to virtuous qualities, guards them, increases them, and exerts diligent application;
it is so called because of the distinction between these four types of activity.
By establishing diligence with a single mind, one is able to perform four tasks: severing present afflictions so they do not arise in the future, and allowing for the growth of wholesome dharmas.
Once arisen, the continuity of the power of skillful means is not lost; that too has fourfold distinctions.
It is also called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*);
they arise according to their respective capacities, and thus they are designated by those names.

He also speaks of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Regarding what was previously stated as "qualities," he speaks of the foundations of mindfulness as in the Sūtras:

body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—whether internal, external, or both—with respect to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). These are called the foundations of mindfulness because of the distinctions among those four kinds of objects, and because of the distinctions in the limits of all those objects.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body has the body as its object, and not other phenomena.

Likewise, when the foundation of mindfulness of feeling is spoken of, it refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling and not others; when the foundation of mindfulness of mind is spoken of, it refers to the foundation of mindfulness of mind and not the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

There are two kinds of conditions for other dharmas: the conditioned condition (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*), which consists of the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
and the disintegrating condition (*bhaṅga-pratyaya*), which consists of bodily sensation (*kāyikī-vedanā*) and both bodily and mental sensation (*sāttvikī-vedanā*).
In this manner, it extends to all dharmas as conditions.
Question: What are the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa)? Answer:
The noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are also like this.

The virtues spoken of there are also called the noble lineages; they are called "noble lineages" because the noble ones take these as their lineage. These dharmas have the nature of being the noble lineage, and thus they are called the noble lineages; because one is born from within this lineage, they are called the noble lineages.
Because there are four types of the arising of craving, four distinctions are taught.
Craving arises because of clothing; the four types are explained at length as in the Sūtra.
Question: How is it that these merits constitute the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) up to the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), and so forth? Answer:
They arise according to their respective powers, and thus they are designated by those names.
These dharmas arise through the power of concentration, and are therefore called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);
they arise through the power of diligence, and are therefore called the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Because mindfulness arises as predominant, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
because contentment arises as predominant, they are called the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Having already explained the commonality of these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) shall now be explained.
Pure faith, diligence, mindfulness, Wisdom, joy, and pliancy,
The factors of enlightenment, and equanimity, Volition, morality,
and concentration. As the Buddha has taught, these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment consist of thirty-seven names, yet only ten entities.
Regarding faith and the other [faculties] therein, they are summarized as in the verse.
Among them, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) are called "faith.

Right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), and the factor of enlightenment of right effort (*samyagvyāyāma-saṃbodhyaṅga*)—these constitute "energy" (*vīrya*).
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—these are called the four foundations of mindfulness regarding mindfulness.
The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, and right view—these are called wisdom.

The factors of enlightenment of joy, tranquility, and equanimity; right intention; virtue as right speech, right action, and right livelihood; the bases of power; the faculty of concentration; the power of concentration; the factor of enlightenment of concentration; and right concentration—these eight branches constitute the factors of concentration.
Question: For what reason is it explained in such manifold ways? Answer:
Abiding in skillful means with one-pointed mind, Whether gentle or sharp, it is likewise so;
In both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, Therefore, thirty-seven factors are taught. Regarding "abiding" (*sthāna*):
because they correctly take objects as their basis, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding "skillful means" (*upāya*): it refers to right skillful means, which is explained as the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Regarding "one-pointed mind" (*ekacitta*): because one dwells within a single state of mind, it is called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Seeing the continuity of weak faculties is termed the "sharpening of faculties" (*indriya*); this is also a faculty. Seeing the continuity of sharp faculties is termed "power" (*bala*).
In this context, the meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*); that which cannot be surpassed by others is called "power" (*bala*).

Because it is attained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is called a "limb of the path" (*mārgāṅga*); because it is seen through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is called a "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*).
It is said that there are thirty-seven.
Because these ten factors each have distinct functions, the Buddha taught thirty-seven.
Among them, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the others are both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted.
Question: How can the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) be with outflows (sāsrava)?
Enlightenment (bodhi) is without outflows (anāsrava); since these [factors] are the vessel for that enlightenment and its retinue, they are therefore called "factors of enlightenment."

Thus, in this context, although these factors are distant from and associated with outflows (*āsrava*), they are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) because they accord with enlightenment; therefore, there is no fault.
In the second dhyāna there are thirty-six; the same applies to the preliminary dhyāna (*anāgamya*).
In the third, fourth, and intermediate dhyānas, there are all thirty-five.
Regarding the thirty-six [factors] of the second dhyāna, "volition" (vitarka) is excluded.
Why? Because this stage is devoid of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
The same applies to the future dhyāna: it also consists of thirty-six factors, excluding the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga). Why is this?
Because it has not yet been accomplished, there is no joy; as I have already explained previously.

Regarding "the fourth, the third, and the intermediate [dhyānas] all consist of thirty-five": in the fourth, third, and intermediate dhyānas, there are thirty-five factors, excluding joy (*prīti*) and correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
The first dhyāna is said to contain all [thirty-seven factors]; the three formless attainments (ārūpya) contain thirty-two;
the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) contains twenty-two; and the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is likewise.
Regarding "the first dhyāna is said to contain all": within the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors are present.
In the three emptinesses, there are thirty-two factors, excluding joy, right thought, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
In the Peak of Existence, there are twenty-two; because all factors of enlightenment and factors of the path are absent there, there are thus twenty-two.

Wherever the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) are mentioned, it should be understood that the path-factors (magganga) therein may be either with-outflow (sāsrava) or without-outflow (anāsrava).

As for the statement "the desire realm is also like this," it means that in the desire realm there are likewise twenty-two factors, which are exclusively with-outflow, because these two locations [the desire realm and the first dhyāna] are entirely characterized by outflows.
Question: In which stages (bhūmi) and of what nature are the four nutriments (āhāra)? Answer:
Among all foods, edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is said in the desire realm to consist of three bases (*āyatana*);
the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*), the volition-food (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*), and the contact-food (*sparśāhāra*)—these foods are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding "among all foods, edible food is said in the desire realm to consist of three bases": edible food consists of the three bases of the desire realm.
Fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
There are thirteen entities; eleven of these entities are tangibles:
the four great elements and the seven kinds of derived matter.
These are: roughness, smoothness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, thirst, as well as odor and taste.
Question: Why are visible form and sound not considered food?
Answer: Seeing and hearing are not "growth.
The meaning of "nourishment" (*āhāra*) is the sense of fully satisfying the faculties and providing great benefit.

Whether through seeing or hearing, by the power of false discrimination, there arises a contact that produces pleasant feeling, which in turn gives rise to joy. That joy, however, cannot nourish or benefit the sense faculties and the primary elements; therefore, it is contact as nutriment that is capable of providing benefit.
It is not that form, sound, odor, or taste can benefit the body apart from conceptual discrimination.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness-food, volition, and contact are said to be with outflows" (*sāsrava*): consciousness, volition, and contact are with outflows; because they maintain the continuity of birth and bind one, being able to draw one toward existence (*bhava*), they are therefore called "nutriments."

Although untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*) and the like greatly benefit the faculties, they cannot draw forth existence (*bhava*); therefore, they eliminate existence and are thus not nutriment (*āhāra*).
There are three reasons why something is called nutriment:
it can draw forth future existence, it continues to draw forth once it has already drawn it forth, and it sustains the physical body; for these reasons, it is called nutriment.
That mental consciousness draws forth future existence;
once the food of morsels and the food of contact have arisen, they sustain all forms of existence.
Alternatively, all types of nutriment are capable of drawing forth existence and sustaining all the sense faculties.
Question: Regarding the various samādhis previously mentioned, which one is the [primary] samādhi?
How many types of transformations does it have?
The answer is:

One should know that there are ten aspects of wishlessness (apraṇihita), two aspects of emptiness (śūnyatā), and four aspects of signlessness (animitta); these are called the noble practices (āryacaryā).

Regarding the ten modes of activity of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*): the wishless samādhi is generally said to have ten modes of activity because it takes the three truths as its object, and thus these ten modes of activity unfold.

Within the truth of suffering, there are two modes—impermanence and suffering. Within the truth of origination, there are four modes as previously explained. Within the truth of the path, there are likewise four modes as previously explained.
Question: For what reason does it not take cessation as its object? Answer:
It is called "wishless" (apraṇihita) because there is no seeking or desiring; this means not taking pleasure in seeking.
What is it that is not wished for?
It refers to suffering (duḥkha).

When those causes are exhausted, they cease to exist; therefore, those causes are also abandoned. Since those causes are exhausted through the cultivation of the path, it is for this reason that the path is the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Thus, this concentration takes suffering and its cause as its object-condition, but does not take cessation as its object-condition.
Alternatively, it is said that one does not aspire toward the conditioned; therefore, it takes the three truths as its object. Among these, the cultivation of the path is like taking bitter medicine.
It should be understood that this is similar to the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because they serve as the direct antidotes to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The samādhi of emptiness has two modes of practice. What are these two?
Emptiness and non-self.
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) consists in the practice of grasping at "I" and "mine. Because it is the antidote to the notion of "I," the practice of non-self (*anātman*) is taught;
because it is the antidote to the notion of "mine," the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught.
Just as those phenomena lack a self, they are therefore without self.

Regarding the statement that the four modes of activity (*caturākāra*) are signless (*animitta*): the signless samādhi (*animittasamādhi*) functions by ceasing these four modes of activity; it excludes conditioned activities (*saṃskṛtākāra*) and takes only phenomena (*dharma*) as its object.
Because these modes of activity are described as signless, this demonstrates the gate of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); therefore, it is exclusively a pure (*anāsrava*) samādhi.
Question: How are the perversions abandoned?
What is their intrinsic nature?
Answer: These four inversions should be known as abandoned through the vision of suffering;
regarding them, the vision of reality establishes their abandonment by means of superior vision.

Regarding the statement that those four inversions should be known as abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*): all four inversions function based upon suffering; therefore, they are abandoned through the vision of suffering. This has already been explained among the three views.
Regarding those who hold these as superior views, these four inversions are a portion of three [of the ten] views; they have the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi*).
In the Sūtras, because of the turbidity of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*), they are called inversions of perception and mind.
Why does one who perceives reality abandon or establish [views]?
Because within the context of superior views, if one attains such superior power, one establishes them erroneously.
For example, the inversion of the view of self is not the view of "mine"; likewise, the inversion of the eternalist view within the extreme views is not the annihilationist view.
The view of grasping at [impermanent things as] pure and [suffering as] pleasant is a perversion of perception. Question:
What is predominant?
Answer: Because it establishes a one-sided perversion, it is therefore a perversion.
Such a perception as that is not, however, every view that is a perversion.
Although wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) involve speculative reasoning and are exclusively inverted, they function by destroying what has been established.

The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) functions through speculative reasoning but is not an exclusively inverted grasping; it takes that which is slightly pure for what is not supreme and takes that which is merely superior for what is truly superior.
The view of "mine" (*mamakāra*) is established based on the power of the view of "self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); therefore, the view of "mine" is not established as an inversion. Question:
The Blessed One has spoken of many views, such as the sixty-two views; by which of these views are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed within the five views. Question:
What is this? The answer is:
To slander reality—this view is called wrong view.
Established as unreal, these two views and this wisdom [are such].

To slander the reality is called a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): if one sees that the reality of existing objects is being slandered by saying they do not exist at all—such as claiming there is no giving and so forth—this constitutes a false view.

Regarding the establishment of the two views and the wise person: within the aggregates, one establishes the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding that which is not truly a self; and one establishes the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) regarding that which is not truly pleasant or pure.
If there is another kind of unreal construction, such as perceiving a person where there is only a tree stump,
this is false knowledge but not false view.
Furthermore, regarding the grasping of precepts and decorum, one perceives a cause where there is no cause.
If one embraces extreme views, relying on the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism;

or if one grasps at non-causes as causes through precepts and observances—such as the view that Maheśvara is the cause, or the practice of the "cow-precept" (go-vrata)—one will cycle through rebirths in the celestial and worldly realms, mistaking them for liberation.
If one embraces extreme views based on the view of permanence or the view of annihilation: to perceive all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as permanent is called the view of permanence.

As it is said regarding those who hold to permanence, they do not understand the continuity of cause and effect; therefore, they establish annihilation within the realm of things, which is called the view of annihilation.
These two views are called the extreme views of grasping (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Apart from these, there are no other views; therefore, one should know that all views are included within these views. Question:
Regarding this view, what is abandoned and what is not?
The answer is:
It is established through denial, and its cause is the view based on the two extremes.
"Turning according to this matter, if one sees that [object], it is then abandoned.
The slanderous wrong views have already been explained.

If one slanders suffering (*duḥkha*), that is said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). Likewise, for those who establish [the truths] such as origination (*samudaya*) and so forth as unreal, two views are taught.

That view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is established upon suffering; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering. If the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) is established upon the vision of suffering as being pleasure and so forth, it is therefore to be known as abandoned through the vision of suffering.

In this way, one should know that the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, if it functions in dependence upon the contaminated (*sāsrava*), is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); if it functions in dependence upon the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
The views of annihilationism and eternalism revolve around suffering; therefore, they are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
